Let us believe that God will keep it going. Some of you have read the words of that aged saint who, on his ninetieth birthday, spoke of all God’s goodness to him — I mean George Müller. What did he say was the secret of his happiness, and of all the blessing God had given him? He said he believed there were two reasons. The first was that, by grace, he had been enabled to keep a good conscience before God day by day. The second was that he loved God’s Word. Ah, yes — a good conscience, which means complete obedience to God day by day, and daily fellowship with God in His Word and in prayer: that is a life of absolute surrender. Such a life has two sides. On one side, it is absolute surrender to do what God wants you to do. On the other side, it is surrender to let God do what He wants to do. First, to do what God wants you to do. Give yourselves up absolutely to the will of God. You know something of that will — not enough, and nowhere near all of it. But say absolutely to the Lord God, “By Your grace I want to do Your will in everything, every moment of every day.” Say, “Lord God, let there be not a word on my tongue except for Your glory, not a stirring of my temper except for Your glory, not a feeling of love or hate in my heart except for Your glory and according to Your blessed will.” Someone asks, “Do you really think that’s possible?” I ask: What has God promised you, and what can God do to fill a vessel that is absolutely surrendered to Him? Oh, God wants to bless you beyond anything you expect. From the beginning, ear hath not heard, neither hath the eye seen, what God hath prepared for them that wait for Him (1 Cor. 2:9). God has prepared unheard-of things, blessings far more wonderful than you can imagine, mightier than you can conceive. They are divine blessings. Oh, say now: “I give myself absolutely to God, to His will, to do only what God wants.” It is God who will enable you to carry out that surrender. And on the other side, come and say, “I give myself absolutely to God, to let Him work in me to will and to do of His good pleasure, as He has promised to do.” Yes, the living God wants to work in His children in a way we cannot understand, but which God’s Word has revealed — and He wants to work in us every moment of the day. God is willing to sustain our life. Only let our absolute surrender be a simple, childlike and unlimited trust. God Blesses When You Surrender This absolute surrender to God will bring wonderful blessing. What Ahab said to his enemy, King Ben-hadad — “My lord, O king, according to thy word I am thine, and all that I have” — shall we not say that to our God and loving Father? If we do say it, God’s blessing will come on us. God wants us to be separate from the world; we are called to come out from the world that hates God. Come out for God, and say, “Lord, anything for You.” If you say that prayerfully, and speak it into God’s ear, He will accept it, and He will teach you what it means. I say it again: God will bless you. You have been praying for blessing. But remember, there must be absolute surrender. You see it at every tea table. Why is tea poured into that cup? Because it is empty and set aside for the tea. But put ink or vinegar or wine in it, and will anyone pour tea into it? And can God fill you, can God bless you, if you are not absolutely surrendered to Him? He cannot. Let us believe that God has wonderful blessings for us, if only we will stand up for God and say — with a trembling will, perhaps, but with a believing heart: “O God, I accept Your demands. I am Yours, and all that I have. Absolute surrender is what my soul gives You, by divine grace.” You may not have the strong, clear sense of deliverance you would like. But humble yourselves in His sight, and admit that you have grieved the Holy Spirit by your self-will, self-confidence and self-effort. Bow humbly before Him as you confess it, and ask Him to break your heart and bring you down into the dust before Him. Then, as you bow before Him, simply accept God’s teaching that in your flesh “there dwelleth no good thing” (Rom. 7:18), and that nothing will help you except another life coming in. You must deny self once and for all. Denying self must be the power of your life every moment, and then Christ will come in and take possession of you. When was Peter set free? When did the change take place? The change began when Peter wept; then the Holy Spirit came down and filled his heart. God the Father loves to give us the power of the Spirit. We have the Spirit of God living within us. We come to God acknowledging that and praising Him for it, and yet confessing how we have grieved the Spirit. Then we bow our knees to the Father and ask Him to strengthen us with all might by the Spirit in the inner man, and to fill us with His mighty power. And as the Spirit reveals Christ to us, Christ comes to live in our hearts for ever, and the self-life is thrown out. Let us bow before God in humility, and in that humility confess before Him the condition of the whole Church. No words can describe the sad state of the Church of Christ on earth. I wish I had words to express what I sometimes feel about it. Just think of the Christians around you. I am not speaking of Christians in name only, or of those who merely profess faith. I am speaking of hundreds and thousands of honest, earnest Christians who are not living a life in the power of God or for His glory. There is so little power, so little devotion or consecration to God, so little grasp of the truth that a Christian is a person utterly surrendered to God’s will! Oh, we need to confess the sins of God’s people around us and to humble ourselves. We are members of that sickly body, and the body’s sickness will hold us back and break us down — unless we come to God and, through confession, separate ourselves from any share in worldliness and in coldness toward one another; unless we give ourselves up to be entirely and wholly God’s. How much Christian work is being done in the spirit of the flesh and in the power of self! How much work goes on day after day in which human energy — our own will and our own ideas about the work — is constantly on display, and in which there is very little waiting on God and on the power of the Holy Spirit! Let us confess it. But as we confess the state of the Church, and the weakness and sinfulness of so much of our work for God, let us come back to ourselves. Who here truly longs to be set free from the power of the self-life? Who truly admits that it is the power of self and the flesh, and is willing to throw it all at the feet of Christ? There is deliverance. I heard of someone who had been an earnest Christian, and who spoke of the “cruel” idea of separation and death. But you don’t think that, do you? What are we to think of separation and death? This: death was Christ’s path to glory. For the joy set before Him He endured the cross. The cross was the birthplace of His everlasting glory. Do you love Christ? Do you long to be in Christ, and yet not be like Him? Let death be the most desirable thing on earth to you — death to self, and fellowship with Christ. Separation — do you think it hard to be called to be completely free from the world, and through that separation to be united to God and His love, and to be made ready to live and walk with God every day? Surely each of us ought to say: “Anything that brings me to separation, to death, for a life of full fellowship with God and Christ.” Come and lay this self-life and flesh-life at the feet of Jesus. Then trust Him. Don’t wear yourselves out trying to understand everything about it. Come in living faith that Christ will come into you with the power of His death and the power of His life. Then the Holy Spirit will bring the whole Christ — Christ crucified and risen and living in glory — into your heart.

fields.title: The Fruit of the Spirit is Love
fields.body_html:
I want to look at the reality of a life filled with the Holy Spirit from its more practical side, and to show how this life will show itself in our daily walk and behaviour.

In Old Testament times, as you know, the Holy Spirit often came upon people as a divine Spirit of revelation, to make known the mysteries of God, or to give power to do the work of God. But He did not live in them then. Today many people want only the Old Testament gift — power for work — and know very little of the New Testament gift of the indwelling Spirit, who brings life and renewal to the whole of our life. When God gives the Holy Spirit, His great aim is to form a holy character. It is the gift of a holy mind and a spiritual disposition, and what we need above everything else is to say:

“I must have the Holy Spirit sanctifying my whole inner life if I am really to live for God’s glory.”

You might say that when Christ promised the Spirit to the disciples, He did it so that they would have power to be witnesses. True. But they received the Holy Spirit with such heavenly power and reality that He took possession of their whole being at once. In that way He made them holy men, fitted to do the work with power, as it had to be done. Christ spoke to the disciples about power, but it was the Spirit filling their whole being that produced the power.

I want now to dwell on the passage in Galatians 5:22:

“The fruit of the Spirit is love.”

We read that “Love is the fulfilling of the law” (Rom. 13:10), and I want to speak about love as a fruit of the Spirit with two aims in view. The first is that this word may be a searchlight in our hearts, giving us a test by which to examine all our thoughts about the Holy Spirit and all our experience of the holy life. Let us test ourselves by this word. Has it been our daily habit to seek to be filled with the Holy Spirit as the Spirit of love? “The fruit of the Spirit is love.” Has it been our experience that the more we have of the Holy Spirit, the more loving we become? When we claim the Holy Spirit, this should be the first thing we expect. The Holy Spirit comes as a Spirit of love.

Oh, if this were true in the Church of Christ, how different her condition would be! May God help us to lay hold of this simple, heavenly truth: the fruit of the Spirit is a love that shows itself in the life. And to the degree that the Holy Spirit truly takes possession of the life, the heart will be filled with real, divine love for everyone.

One of the great reasons why God cannot bless His Church is the lack of love. When the body is divided, there can be no strength. In the time of the great religious wars, when Holland stood up so nobly against Spain, one of the Dutch mottoes was: “Unity gives strength.” Only when God’s people stand as one body — one before God in the fellowship of love, one toward each other in deep affection, one before the world in a love the world can see — only then will they have power to obtain the blessing they ask of God. Remember: if a vessel that ought to be whole is cracked into many pieces, it cannot be filled. You can take a broken fragment, one part of a vessel, and scoop a little water into it; but if you want the vessel full, it must be whole. That is literally true of Christ’s Church. If there is one thing we must still pray for, it is this: “Lord, melt us together into one by the power of the Holy Spirit. Let the Holy Spirit, who at Pentecost made them all of one heart and one soul, do His blessed work among us.” Praise God, we can love one another with a divine love, for “the fruit of the Spirit is love.” Give yourselves up to love, and the Holy Spirit will come; receive the Spirit, and He will teach you to love more.

God Is Love

Now, why is the fruit of the Spirit love? Because God is love (1 John 4:8).

And what does that mean?

It is God’s very nature and being to delight in giving Himself. There is no selfishness in God; God keeps nothing to Himself. It is His nature to be always giving. You see it in the sun and the moon and the stars, in every flower, in every bird in the air, in every fish in the sea. God gives life to His creatures. And the angels around His throne, the seraphim and cherubim who are flames of fire — where does their glory come from? It is because God is love, and He shares His brightness and His blessedness with them. And we, His redeemed children — God delights to pour His love into us. Why? Because, as I said, God keeps nothing for Himself. From eternity God had His only begotten Son, and the Father gave Him all things; nothing God had was held back. “God is love.”

One of the old Church fathers said that there is no better way to understand the Trinity than as a revelation of divine love. The Father is the loving One, the Fountain of love. The Son is the beloved One, the Reservoir of love, into whom that love was poured. And the Spirit is the living love that unites them both and then overflows into this world. The Spirit of Pentecost, the Spirit of the Father and the Spirit of the Son, is love. And when the Holy Spirit comes to us and to others, will He be any less a Spirit of love than He is in God? Impossible; He cannot change His nature. The Spirit of God is love, and “the fruit of the Spirit is love.”

Mankind Needs Love

Why is that so? Because love was mankind’s one great need, and that was what Christ’s redemption came to achieve: to restore love to this world.

When man sinned, why did he sin? Selfishness won — he sought himself instead of God. And just look! Adam immediately starts blaming the woman for leading him astray. Love for God had gone; love for others was lost. Look again: of Adam’s first two children, one becomes his brother’s murderer.

Doesn’t that teach us that sin had robbed the world of love? Ah, what proof the history of the world has been that love was lost! There may have been beautiful examples of love even among the heathen, but only as a small remnant of what had been lost. One of the worst things sin did to man was to make him selfish, and selfishness cannot love.

The Lord Jesus Christ came down from heaven as the Son of God’s love. “God so loved the world that He gave His only begotten Son” (John 3:16). God’s Son came to show what love is. He lived a life of love here on earth — in fellowship with His disciples, in compassion for the poor and wretched, in love even for His enemies — and He died the death of love. And when He went to heaven, whom did He send down? The Spirit of love, to come and drive out selfishness and envy and pride, and to bring the love of God into human hearts. “The fruit of the Spirit is love.”

And what prepared the way for the promise of the Holy Spirit? You know that promise from the fourteenth chapter of John’s Gospel. But remember what comes before it in the thirteenth chapter. Before Christ promised the Holy Spirit, He gave a new commandment, and He said wonderful things about it. One of them was: “Even as I have loved you, so love ye one another.” His dying love was to be the only rule for how they behaved and dealt with one another. What a message for those fishermen, those men full of pride and selfishness! “Learn to love one another,” Christ said, “as I have loved you.” And by the grace of God they did. When Pentecost came, they were of one heart and one soul. Christ did it for them.

And now He calls us to live and walk in love. He requires that even if someone hates you, you still love him. Nothing in heaven or on earth can conquer true love. The more hatred there is, the more love triumphs through it all and shows its true nature. This is the love Christ commanded His disciples to practise.

What else did He say? “By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another” (John 13:35).

You all know what it is to wear a badge. And in effect Christ said to His disciples, “I am giving you a badge, and that badge is love. That is to be your mark. It is the only thing in heaven or on earth by which people can know Me.”

Don’t we begin to fear that love has fled from the earth? That if we were to ask the world, “Have you seen us wearing the badge of love?” the world would answer, “No. What we have heard about the Church of Christ is that there is hardly a place without quarrelling and division.” Let us ask God with one heart that we may wear the badge of Jesus’ love. God is able to give it.

Love Conquers Selfishness

“The fruit of the Spirit is love.” Why? Because nothing but love can drive out and conquer our selfishness.

Self — thinking of ourselves and seeking our own interests — is the great curse, whether in our relationship to God, to people in general, or to fellow Christians. Self is our greatest curse. But praise God, Christ came to redeem us from self. We sometimes talk about deliverance from the self-life — and thank God for every word that can be said about it to help us. But I am afraid some people think deliverance from the self-life means they will no longer have any trouble serving God. They forget that deliverance from the self-life means being a vessel overflowing with love to everyone all day long.

And that is why many people pray for the power of the Holy Spirit and receive something — but oh, so little! They prayed for power for work and power for blessing, but they did not pray for power for complete deliverance from self. That means deliverance not only from the self-righteous self in our dealings with God, but from the unloving self in our dealings with people. And there is deliverance. “The fruit of the Spirit is love.” I bring you Christ’s glorious promise that He is able to fill our hearts with love.

Many of us try hard at times to love. We try to force ourselves to love, and I don’t say that is wrong; it is better than nothing. But it always ends very sadly. Such a person has to confess, “I fail all the time.” And why? The reason is simply this: they have never learned to believe and accept the truth that the Holy Spirit can pour God’s love into their hearts. How often that blessed text has been narrowed down! — “The love of God is shed abroad in our hearts” (Rom. 5:5). It has often been taken to mean only the love of God for me. Oh, what a limitation! That is only the beginning. The love of God is always the love of God in its entirety, in its fullness, as a power living within: a love of God for me that springs back to Him in love and overflows to others in love. God’s love for me, my love for God, and my love for others — the three are one; you cannot separate them.

Do believe that the love of God can be poured into your heart and mine, so that we can love all day long.

“Ah!” you say, “how little I have understood that!”

Why is a lamb always gentle? Because that is its nature. Does it cost the lamb any effort to be gentle? No. Why not? It is so lovely and gentle. Does a lamb have to study how to be gentle? No. Why does it come so easily? It is its nature. And the wolf — why does it cost the wolf no effort to be cruel and to sink its fangs into the poor lamb or sheep? Because that is its nature. It does not have to summon up its courage; the wolf-nature is there.

So how can I learn to love? Never, until the Spirit of God fills my heart with God’s love, and I begin to long for God’s love in a very different way from the selfish way I have sought it — as comfort and joy and happiness and pleasure for myself. Never, until I begin to learn that “God is love,” and to claim that love and receive it as a power living in me for self-sacrifice. Never, until I begin to see that my glory and my blessedness lie in being like God and like Christ, giving up everything in myself for the sake of others. May God teach us that! Oh, the divine blessedness of the love with which the Holy Spirit can fill our hearts! “The fruit of the Spirit is love.”

Love Is God’s Gift

Once again I ask, why must this be so? And my answer is: without it we cannot live the daily life of love.

How often, when we speak about the consecrated life, we have to speak about temper! And some people have said,

“You make too much of temper.”

I don’t think we can make too much of it. Think for a moment about a clock and what its hands mean. The hands tell me what is going on inside the clock. If I see the hands standing still, or pointing wrongly, or the clock running slow or fast, I say that something inside the clock is not working properly. Temper is just like that: it reveals what is inside. Temper shows whether or not the love of Christ is filling the heart. How many people find it easier to be holy and happy in church, or at a prayer meeting, or in work for the Lord — diligent, earnest work — than in daily life with their wife and children! Easier to be holy and happy outside the home than inside it! Where is the love of God? In Christ. God has prepared a wonderful redemption for us in Christ, and He longs to make something supernatural of us. Have we learned to long for it, and ask for it, and expect it in all its fullness?

Then there is the tongue! We sometimes mention the tongue when we talk about the higher life and the restful life — but just think how much freedom many Christians give their tongues. They say,

“I have a right to think what I like.”

When they talk about one another, when they talk about their neighbours, when they talk about other Christians, how often there are cutting remarks! God keep me from saying anything unloving; God shut my mouth if I am not going to speak in tender love. But what I am saying is a fact. How often, among Christians who are joined together in work, we find sharp criticism, harsh judgment, hasty opinions, unloving words, secret contempt and secret condemnation of one another! Oh, just as a mother’s love covers her children, delights in them and has the tenderest compassion for their weaknesses and failures, so there ought to be in every believer’s heart a motherly love toward every brother and sister in Christ. Have you aimed at that? Have you sought it? Have you ever pleaded for it? Jesus Christ said, “As I have loved you . . . love one another” (John 13:34). And He did not place that among the other commandments. In effect He said:

“That is a new commandment, the one commandment: Love one another as I have loved you” (John 13:34).

It is in our daily life and conduct that the fruit of the Spirit is love. From love come all the graces and virtues in which love shows itself: joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness; no sharpness or hardness in your tone, no unkindness or selfishness; meekness before God and people. You see that these are all the gentler virtues. As I read those words in Colossians, “Put on therefore as the elect of God, holy and beloved, bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind, meekness, longsuffering” (Col. 3:12), I have often thought that if we had written it, we would have put the manly virtues in the foreground — zeal, courage and diligence. But we need to see how the gentler virtues, the most womanly ones, are especially bound up with dependence on the Holy Spirit. These are truly heavenly graces. They were never found in the heathen world. Christ had to come from heaven to teach them to us. Your blessedness is longsuffering, meekness and kindness; your glory is humility before God. The fruit of the Spirit that He brought from heaven out of the heart of the crucified Christ, and that He produces in our hearts, is first and foremost — love.

You know what John says: “No man hath seen God at any time. If we love one another, God dwelleth in us” (1 John 4:12). In other words, I cannot see God, but to make up for it I can see my brother, and if I love him, God lives in me. Is that really true? That I cannot see God, but I must love my brother, and God will live in me? Loving my brother is the way to real fellowship with God. You know what John says further in that most solemn test: “If a man say, I love God, and hateth his brother, he is a liar; for he that loveth not his brother whom he hath seen, how can he love God whom he hath not seen?” (1 John 4:20). Here is a brother, a most unlovable man. He irritates you every time you meet him. His temperament is the very opposite of yours. You are a careful businessman, and you have to deal with him in your business. He is extremely untidy and unbusinesslike. You say,

“I cannot love him.”

Oh, friend, you have not learned the lesson Christ most wanted to teach. Whatever a man may be like, you are to love him. Love is to be the fruit of the Spirit all day and every day. Yes, listen! If a man loves not his brother whom he hath seen — if you do not love that unlovable man whom you have seen, how can you love God whom you have not seen? You can fool yourself with beautiful thoughts about loving God. You must prove your love for God by your love for your brother; that is the one standard by which God will judge your love for Him. If the love of God is in your heart, you will love your brother. The fruit of the Spirit is love.

And why is it that God’s Holy Spirit cannot come in power? Is it not possible?

You remember the comparison I used when I spoke about the vessel. I can scoop a little water into a broken fragment, a piece of a vessel; but if a vessel is to be full, it must be unbroken. And wherever God’s children come together, whatever church or mission or society they belong to, they must love one another intensely, or the Spirit of God cannot do His work. We talk about grieving the Spirit of God by worldliness and ritualism and formality and error and indifference. But I tell you, the one thing that grieves God’s Spirit above all else is this lack of love. Let every heart search itself, and ask God to search it.

Our Love Shows God’s Power

Why are we taught that “the fruit of the Spirit is love”? Because the Spirit of God has come to make our daily life a display of divine power and a revelation of what God can do for His children.

In the second and fourth chapters of Acts we read that the disciples were of one heart and one soul. In the three years they had walked with Christ, they had never been of that spirit. All Christ’s teaching could not make them of one heart and one soul. But the Holy Spirit came from heaven and poured the love of God into their hearts, and they were of one heart and one soul. The same Holy Spirit who brought the love of heaven into their hearts must fill us too. Nothing less will do. Someone might preach love for three years with the tongue of an angel, just as Christ did, but that would not teach anyone to love unless the power of the Holy Spirit came upon him and brought the love of heaven into his heart.

Think of the Church as a whole. What divisions! Think of the different denominations. Take the question of holiness, the question of the cleansing blood, the question of the baptism of the Spirit — what differences such questions cause among dear believers! That there are differences of opinion does not trouble me. We do not all have the same constitution, temperament and mind. But how often the holiest truths of God’s Word have produced hatred, bitterness, contempt, division and lovelessness! Our doctrines and our creeds have mattered more to us than love. We often think we are standing bravely for the truth, and we forget God’s command to speak the truth in love. It was like that at the time of the Reformation between the Lutheran and Calvinist churches. What bitterness there was then over the Lord’s Supper, which was meant to be the bond of union among all believers! And so, down the ages, the very dearest truths of God have become mountains that separate us.

If we want to pray with power, if we want to expect the Holy Spirit to come down in power, if we truly want God to pour out His Spirit, we must enter into a covenant with God that we will love one another with a heavenly love.

Are you ready for that? The only true love is a love large enough to take in all God’s children — the most unloving and unlovable, the unworthy, the unbearable and the trying. If my vow of absolute surrender to God was genuine, then it must mean absolute surrender to divine love, so that it can fill me; it must mean becoming a servant of love, loving every child of God around me. “The fruit of the Spirit is love.”

Oh, God did something wonderful when He gave Christ, at His right hand, the Holy Spirit to come down from the heart of the Father and His everlasting love. And how we have reduced the Holy Spirit to a mere power for getting our work done! God forgive us! Oh, that the Holy Spirit might be honoured as a power that fills us with the very life and nature of God and of Christ!

Christian Work Requires Love

“The fruit of the Spirit is love.” Once again I ask, why is it so? And the answer comes: love is the only power in which Christians can really do their work.

Yes, that is what we need. We need not only a love that binds us to one another; we need a divine love in our work for the lost around us. Oh, don’t we often take on a great deal of work in the same way people take on charitable work — out of a natural feeling of compassion for others? Don’t we often take on Christian work because our minister or a friend asks us to? And don’t we often do Christian work with a certain zeal, but without ever having had a baptism of love?

People often ask, “What is the baptism of fire?”

I have answered more than once: I know no fire like the fire of God, the fire of everlasting love that consumed the sacrifice on Calvary. The baptism of love is what the Church needs. To get it, we must begin at once to fall on our faces before God in confession and plead:

“Lord, let love from heaven flow down into my heart. I am giving up my life to pray and to live as someone who has given himself up for the everlasting love to live in him and fill him.”

Ah, yes — if the love of God were in our hearts, what a difference it would make! There are hundreds of believers who say,

“I work for Christ, and I feel I could work much harder, but I don’t have the gift. I don’t know how or where to begin. I don’t know what I can do.”

Brother, sister, ask God to baptise you with the Spirit of love, and love will find its way. Love is a fire that will burn through every difficulty. You may be shy and hesitant and unable to speak well, but love can burn through everything. God fill us with love! We need it for our work.

You have read many moving stories of love in action, and you have said, “How beautiful!” I heard one not long ago. A lady had been asked to speak at a rescue home where a number of poor women lived. When she arrived and went to the window with the matron, she saw a wretched figure sitting outside and asked,

“Who is that?”

The matron answered, “She has come into the house thirty or forty times, and she has always left again. Nothing can be done with her; she is so low and so hard.”

But the lady said, “She must come in.”

The matron then said, “We have been waiting for you. Everyone has gathered, and you have only an hour for your talk.”

The lady replied, “No, this matters more.” She went outside to where the woman was sitting and said,

“My sister, what is the matter?”

“I’m not your sister,” came the reply.

Then the lady laid her hand on her and said, “Yes, I am your sister, and I love you.” And she went on speaking like that until the poor woman’s heart was touched.

The conversation went on for some time, and the people inside waited patiently. At last the lady brought the woman into the room. There she was, the poor, wretched, degraded creature, full of shame. She would not sit on a chair, but sat on a stool beside the speaker’s seat, and the lady let her lean against her, with her arms around the poor woman’s neck, while she spoke to the gathered people. And that love touched the woman’s heart. She had found someone who truly loved her, and that love opened the way to the love of Jesus.

Praise God! there is love on earth in the hearts of God’s children — but oh, that there were more!

O God, baptise our ministers with a tender love — and our missionaries, our Bible readers, our workers, and our young men’s and young women’s associations. Oh, that God would begin with us now and baptise us with heavenly love!

Love Inspires Intercession

Once again: only love can fit us for the work of intercession.

I have said that love must fit us for our work. Do you know what the hardest and most important work is that has to be done for this sinful world? It is the work of intercession — going to God and taking time to lay hold of Him.

A man may be an earnest Christian, an earnest minister; he may do much good. But how often, sadly, he has to confess that he knows very little of what it means to wait in God’s presence. May God give us the great gift of an intercessory spirit, a spirit of prayer and supplication! I ask you in the name of Jesus not to let a single day go by without praying for all the saints, for all God’s people.

I find there are Christians who think little of that. I find prayer unions that pray for their own members, but not for all believers. I beg you, take time to pray for the Church of Christ. It is right to pray for the heathen, as I have already said — God help us to pray for them more. It is right to pray for missionaries, for evangelistic work and for the unconverted. But Paul did not tell people to pray for the heathen or the unconverted. Paul told them to pray for believers. Make this your first prayer every day: “Lord, bless Your saints everywhere.”

The condition of Christ’s Church is low beyond words. Plead for God’s people, that He would visit them; plead for one another; plead for all believers who are trying to work for God. Let love fill your heart. Ask Christ to pour it into you afresh every day. Seek to have it brought into you by the Holy Spirit of God: I am set apart for the Holy Spirit, and the fruit of the Spirit is love. God help us to understand it.

May God grant that day by day we learn to wait on Him more quietly. Let us not wait on God only for ourselves, or the power to do it will soon be lost. Let us give ourselves to the ministry and the love of intercession, and pray more for God’s people — for God’s people all around us, for the Spirit of love in ourselves and in them, and for the work of God we are part of. The answer will surely come, and our waiting on God will become a source of untold blessing and power. “The fruit of the Spirit is love.”

Do you have a lack of love to confess before God? Then confess it, and say before Him, “O Lord, my lack of heart, my lack of love — I confess it.” And then, as you lay that lack at His feet, believe that the blood cleanses you, that Jesus comes in His mighty, cleansing, saving power to set you free, and that He will give His Holy Spirit.

“The fruit of the Spirit is love.”
fields.body_text: I want to look at the reality of a life filled with the Holy Spirit from its more practical side, and to show how this life will show itself in our daily walk and behaviour. In Old Testament times, as you know, the Holy Spirit often came upon people as a divine Spirit of revelation, to make known the mysteries of God, or to give power to do the work of God. But He did not live in them then. Today many people want only the Old Testament gift — power for work — and know very little of the New Testament gift of the indwelling Spirit, who brings life and renewal to the whole of our life. When God gives the Holy Spirit, His great aim is to form a holy character. It is the gift of a holy mind and a spiritual disposition, and what we need above everything else is to say: “I must have the Holy Spirit sanctifying my whole inner life if I am really to live for God’s glory.” You might say that when Christ promised the Spirit to the disciples, He did it so that they would have power to be witnesses. True. But they received the Holy Spirit with such heavenly power and reality that He took possession of their whole being at once. In that way He made them holy men, fitted to do the work with power, as it had to be done. Christ spoke to the disciples about power, but it was the Spirit filling their whole being that produced the power. I want now to dwell on the passage in Galatians 5:22: “The fruit of the Spirit is love.” We read that “Love is the fulfilling of the law” (Rom. 13:10), and I want to speak about love as a fruit of the Spirit with two aims in view. The first is that this word may be a searchlight in our hearts, giving us a test by which to examine all our thoughts about the Holy Spirit and all our experience of the holy life. Let us test ourselves by this word. Has it been our daily habit to seek to be filled with the Holy Spirit as the Spirit of love? “The fruit of the Spirit is love.” Has it been our experience that the more we have of the Holy Spirit, the more loving we become? When we claim the Holy Spirit, this should be the first thing we expect. The Holy Spirit comes as a Spirit of love. Oh, if this were true in the Church of Christ, how different her condition would be! May God help us to lay hold of this simple, heavenly truth: the fruit of the Spirit is a love that shows itself in the life. And to the degree that the Holy Spirit truly takes possession of the life, the heart will be filled with real, divine love for everyone. One of the great reasons why God cannot bless His Church is the lack of love. When the body is divided, there can be no strength. In the time of the great religious wars, when Holland stood up so nobly against Spain, one of the Dutch mottoes was: “Unity gives strength.” Only when God’s people stand as one body — one before God in the fellowship of love, one toward each other in deep affection, one before the world in a love the world can see — only then will they have power to obtain the blessing they ask of God. Remember: if a vessel that ought to be whole is cracked into many pieces, it cannot be filled. You can take a broken fragment, one part of a vessel, and scoop a little water into it; but if you want the vessel full, it must be whole. That is literally true of Christ’s Church. If there is one thing we must still pray for, it is this: “Lord, melt us together into one by the power of the Holy Spirit. Let the Holy Spirit, who at Pentecost made them all of one heart and one soul, do His blessed work among us.” Praise God, we can love one another with a divine love, for “the fruit of the Spirit is love.” Give yourselves up to love, and the Holy Spirit will come; receive the Spirit, and He will teach you to love more. God Is Love Now, why is the fruit of the Spirit love? Because God is love (1 John 4:8). And what does that mean? It is God’s very nature and being to delight in giving Himself. There is no selfishness in God; God keeps nothing to Himself. It is His nature to be always giving. You see it in the sun and the moon and the stars, in every flower, in every bird in the air, in every fish in the sea. God gives life to His creatures. And the angels around His throne, the seraphim and cherubim who are flames of fire — where does their glory come from? It is because God is love, and He shares His brightness and His blessedness with them. And we, His redeemed children — God delights to pour His love into us. Why? Because, as I said, God keeps nothing for Himself. From eternity God had His only begotten Son, and the Father gave Him all things; nothing God had was held back. “God is love.” One of the old Church fathers said that there is no better way to understand the Trinity than as a revelation of divine love. The Father is the loving One, the Fountain of love. The Son is the beloved One, the Reservoir of love, into whom that love was poured. And the Spirit is the living love that unites them both and then overflows into this world. The Spirit of Pentecost, the Spirit of the Father and the Spirit of the Son, is love. And when the Holy Spirit comes to us and to others, will He be any less a Spirit of love than He is in God? Impossible; He cannot change His nature. The Spirit of God is love, and “the fruit of the Spirit is love.” Mankind Needs Love Why is that so? Because love was mankind’s one great need, and that was what Christ’s redemption came to achieve: to restore love to this world. When man sinned, why did he sin? Selfishness won — he sought himself instead of God. And just look! Adam immediately starts blaming the woman for leading him astray. Love for God had gone; love for others was lost. Look again: of Adam’s first two children, one becomes his brother’s murderer. Doesn’t that teach us that sin had robbed the world of love? Ah, what proof the history of the world has been that love was lost! There may have been beautiful examples of love even among the heathen, but only as a small remnant of what had been lost. One of the worst things sin did to man was to make him selfish, and selfishness cannot love. The Lord Jesus Christ came down from heaven as the Son of God’s love. “God so loved the world that He gave His only begotten Son” (John 3:16). God’s Son came to show what love is. He lived a life of love here on earth — in fellowship with His disciples, in compassion for the poor and wretched, in love even for His enemies — and He died the death of love. And when He went to heaven, whom did He send down? The Spirit of love, to come and drive out selfishness and envy and pride, and to bring the love of God into human hearts. “The fruit of the Spirit is love.” And what prepared the way for the promise of the Holy Spirit? You know that promise from the fourteenth chapter of John’s Gospel. But remember what comes before it in the thirteenth chapter. Before Christ promised the Holy Spirit, He gave a new commandment, and He said wonderful things about it. One of them was: “Even as I have loved you, so love ye one another.” His dying love was to be the only rule for how they behaved and dealt with one another. What a message for those fishermen, those men full of pride and selfishness! “Learn to love one another,” Christ said, “as I have loved you.” And by the grace of God they did. When Pentecost came, they were of one heart and one soul. Christ did it for them. And now He calls us to live and walk in love. He requires that even if someone hates you, you still love him. Nothing in heaven or on earth can conquer true love. The more hatred there is, the more love triumphs through it all and shows its true nature. This is the love Christ commanded His disciples to practise. What else did He say? “By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another” (John 13:35). You all know what it is to wear a badge. And in effect Christ said to His disciples, “I am giving you a badge, and that badge is love. That is to be your mark. It is the only thing in heaven or on earth by which people can know Me.” Don’t we begin to fear that love has fled from the earth? That if we were to ask the world, “Have you seen us wearing the badge of love?” the world would answer, “No. What we have heard about the Church of Christ is that there is hardly a place without quarrelling and division.” Let us ask God with one heart that we may wear the badge of Jesus’ love. God is able to give it. Love Conquers Selfishness “The fruit of the Spirit is love.” Why? Because nothing but love can drive out and conquer our selfishness. Self — thinking of ourselves and seeking our own interests — is the great curse, whether in our relationship to God, to people in general, or to fellow Christians. Self is our greatest curse. But praise God, Christ came to redeem us from self. We sometimes talk about deliverance from the self-life — and thank God for every word that can be said about it to help us. But I am afraid some people think deliverance from the self-life means they will no longer have any trouble serving God. They forget that deliverance from the self-life means being a vessel overflowing with love to everyone all day long. And that is why many people pray for the power of the Holy Spirit and receive something — but oh, so little! They prayed for power for work and power for blessing, but they did not pray for power for complete deliverance from self. That means deliverance not only from the self-righteous self in our dealings with God, but from the unloving self in our dealings with people. And there is deliverance. “The fruit of the Spirit is love.” I bring you Christ’s glorious promise that He is able to fill our hearts with love. Many of us try hard at times to love. We try to force ourselves to love, and I don’t say that is wrong; it is better than nothing. But it always ends very sadly. Such a person has to confess, “I fail all the time.” And why? The reason is simply this: they have never learned to believe and accept the truth that the Holy Spirit can pour God’s love into their hearts. How often that blessed text has been narrowed down! — “The love of God is shed abroad in our hearts” (Rom. 5:5). It has often been taken to mean only the love of God for me. Oh, what a limitation! That is only the beginning. The love of God is always the love of God in its entirety, in its fullness, as a power living within: a love of God for me that springs back to Him in love and overflows to others in love. God’s love for me, my love for God, and my love for others — the three are one; you cannot separate them. Do believe that the love of God can be poured into your heart and mine, so that we can love all day long. “Ah!” you say, “how little I have understood that!” Why is a lamb always gentle? Because that is its nature. Does it cost the lamb any effort to be gentle? No. Why not? It is so lovely and gentle. Does a lamb have to study how to be gentle? No. Why does it come so easily? It is its nature. And the wolf — why does it cost the wolf no effort to be cruel and to sink its fangs into the poor lamb or sheep? Because that is its nature. It does not have to summon up its courage; the wolf-nature is there. So how can I learn to love? Never, until the Spirit of God fills my heart with God’s love, and I begin to long for God’s love in a very different way from the selfish way I have sought it — as comfort and joy and happiness and pleasure for myself. Never, until I begin to learn that “God is love,” and to claim that love and receive it as a power living in me for self-sacrifice. Never, until I begin to see that my glory and my blessedness lie in being like God and like Christ, giving up everything in myself for the sake of others. May God teach us that! Oh, the divine blessedness of the love with which the Holy Spirit can fill our hearts! “The fruit of the Spirit is love.” Love Is God’s Gift Once again I ask, why must this be so? And my answer is: without it we cannot live the daily life of love. How often, when we speak about the consecrated life, we have to speak about temper! And some people have said, “You make too much of temper.” I don’t think we can make too much of it. Think for a moment about a clock and what its hands mean. The hands tell me what is going on inside the clock. If I see the hands standing still, or pointing wrongly, or the clock running slow or fast, I say that something inside the clock is not working properly. Temper is just like that: it reveals what is inside. Temper shows whether or not the love of Christ is filling the heart. How many people find it easier to be holy and happy in church, or at a prayer meeting, or in work for the Lord — diligent, earnest work — than in daily life with their wife and children! Easier to be holy and happy outside the home than inside it! Where is the love of God? In Christ. God has prepared a wonderful redemption for us in Christ, and He longs to make something supernatural of us. Have we learned to long for it, and ask for it, and expect it in all its fullness? Then there is the tongue! We sometimes mention the tongue when we talk about the higher life and the restful life — but just think how much freedom many Christians give their tongues. They say, “I have a right to think what I like.” When they talk about one another, when they talk about their neighbours, when they talk about other Christians, how often there are cutting remarks! God keep me from saying anything unloving; God shut my mouth if I am not going to speak in tender love. But what I am saying is a fact. How often, among Christians who are joined together in work, we find sharp criticism, harsh judgment, hasty opinions, unloving words, secret contempt and secret condemnation of one another! Oh, just as a mother’s love covers her children, delights in them and has the tenderest compassion for their weaknesses and failures, so there ought to be in every believer’s heart a motherly love toward every brother and sister in Christ. Have you aimed at that? Have you sought it? Have you ever pleaded for it? Jesus Christ said, “As I have loved you . . . love one another” (John 13:34). And He did not place that among the other commandments. In effect He said: “That is a new commandment, the one commandment: Love one another as I have loved you” (John 13:34). It is in our daily life and conduct that the fruit of the Spirit is love. From love come all the graces and virtues in which love shows itself: joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness; no sharpness or hardness in your tone, no unkindness or selfishness; meekness before God and people. You see that these are all the gentler virtues. As I read those words in Colossians, “Put on therefore as the elect of God, holy and beloved, bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind, meekness, longsuffering” (Col. 3:12), I have often thought that if we had written it, we would have put the manly virtues in the foreground — zeal, courage and diligence. But we need to see how the gentler virtues, the most womanly ones, are especially bound up with dependence on the Holy Spirit. These are truly heavenly graces. They were never found in the heathen world. Christ had to come from heaven to teach them to us. Your blessedness is longsuffering, meekness and kindness; your glory is humility before God. The fruit of the Spirit that He brought from heaven out of the heart of the crucified Christ, and that He produces in our hearts, is first and foremost — love. You know what John says: “No man hath seen God at any time. If we love one another, God dwelleth in us” (1 John 4:12). In other words, I cannot see God, but to make up for it I can see my brother, and if I love him, God lives in me. Is that really true? That I cannot see God, but I must love my brother, and God will live in me? Loving my brother is the way to real fellowship with God. You know what John says further in that most solemn test: “If a man say, I love God, and hateth his brother, he is a liar; for he that loveth not his brother whom he hath seen, how can he love God whom he hath not seen?” (1 John 4:20). Here is a brother, a most unlovable man. He irritates you every time you meet him. His temperament is the very opposite of yours. You are a careful businessman, and you have to deal with him in your business. He is extremely untidy and unbusinesslike. You say, “I cannot love him.” Oh, friend, you have not learned the lesson Christ most wanted to teach. Whatever a man may be like, you are to love him. Love is to be the fruit of the Spirit all day and every day. Yes, listen! If a man loves not his brother whom he hath seen — if you do not love that unlovable man whom you have seen, how can you love God whom you have not seen? You can fool yourself with beautiful thoughts about loving God. You must prove your love for God by your love for your brother; that is the one standard by which God will judge your love for Him. If the love of God is in your heart, you will love your brother. The fruit of the Spirit is love. And why is it that God’s Holy Spirit cannot come in power? Is it not possible? You remember the comparison I used when I spoke about the vessel. I can scoop a little water into a broken fragment, a piece of a vessel; but if a vessel is to be full, it must be unbroken. And wherever God’s children come together, whatever church or mission or society they belong to, they must love one another intensely, or the Spirit of God cannot do His work. We talk about grieving the Spirit of God by worldliness and ritualism and formality and error and indifference. But I tell you, the one thing that grieves God’s Spirit above all else is this lack of love. Let every heart search itself, and ask God to search it. Our Love Shows God’s Power Why are we taught that “the fruit of the Spirit is love”? Because the Spirit of God has come to make our daily life a display of divine power and a revelation of what God can do for His children. In the second and fourth chapters of Acts we read that the disciples were of one heart and one soul. In the three years they had walked with Christ, they had never been of that spirit. All Christ’s teaching could not make them of one heart and one soul. But the Holy Spirit came from heaven and poured the love of God into their hearts, and they were of one heart and one soul. The same Holy Spirit who brought the love of heaven into their hearts must fill us too. Nothing less will do. Someone might preach love for three years with the tongue of an angel, just as Christ did, but that would not teach anyone to love unless the power of the Holy Spirit came upon him and brought the love of heaven into his heart. Think of the Church as a whole. What divisions! Think of the different denominations. Take the question of holiness, the question of the cleansing blood, the question of the baptism of the Spirit — what differences such questions cause among dear believers! That there are differences of opinion does not trouble me. We do not all have the same constitution, temperament and mind. But how often the holiest truths of God’s Word have produced hatred, bitterness, contempt, division and lovelessness! Our doctrines and our creeds have mattered more to us than love. We often think we are standing bravely for the truth, and we forget God’s command to speak the truth in love. It was like that at the time of the Reformation between the Lutheran and Calvinist churches. What bitterness there was then over the Lord’s Supper, which was meant to be the bond of union among all believers! And so, down the ages, the very dearest truths of God have become mountains that separate us. If we want to pray with power, if we want to expect the Holy Spirit to come down in power, if we truly want God to pour out His Spirit, we must enter into a covenant with God that we will love one another with a heavenly love. Are you ready for that? The only true love is a love large enough to take in all God’s children — the most unloving and unlovable, the unworthy, the unbearable and the trying. If my vow of absolute surrender to God was genuine, then it must mean absolute surrender to divine love, so that it can fill me; it must mean becoming a servant of love, loving every child of God around me. “The fruit of the Spirit is love.” Oh, God did something wonderful when He gave Christ, at His right hand, the Holy Spirit to come down from the heart of the Father and His everlasting love. And how we have reduced the Holy Spirit to a mere power for getting our work done! God forgive us! Oh, that the Holy Spirit might be honoured as a power that fills us with the very life and nature of God and of Christ! Christian Work Requires Love “The fruit of the Spirit is love.” Once again I ask, why is it so? And the answer comes: love is the only power in which Christians can really do their work. Yes, that is what we need. We need not only a love that binds us to one another; we need a divine love in our work for the lost around us. Oh, don’t we often take on a great deal of work in the same way people take on charitable work — out of a natural feeling of compassion for others? Don’t we often take on Christian work because our minister or a friend asks us to? And don’t we often do Christian work with a certain zeal, but without ever having had a baptism of love? People often ask, “What is the baptism of fire?” I have answered more than once: I know no fire like the fire of God, the fire of everlasting love that consumed the sacrifice on Calvary. The baptism of love is what the Church needs. To get it, we must begin at once to fall on our faces before God in confession and plead: “Lord, let love from heaven flow down into my heart. I am giving up my life to pray and to live as someone who has given himself up for the everlasting love to live in him and fill him.” Ah, yes — if the love of God were in our hearts, what a difference it would make! There are hundreds of believers who say, “I work for Christ, and I feel I could work much harder, but I don’t have the gift. I don’t know how or where to begin. I don’t know what I can do.” Brother, sister, ask God to baptise you with the Spirit of love, and love will find its way. Love is a fire that will burn through every difficulty. You may be shy and hesitant and unable to speak well, but love can burn through everything. God fill us with love! We need it for our work. You have read many moving stories of love in action, and you have said, “How beautiful!” I heard one not long ago. A lady had been asked to speak at a rescue home where a number of poor women lived. When she arrived and went to the window with the matron, she saw a wretched figure sitting outside and asked, “Who is that?” The matron answered, “She has come into the house thirty or forty times, and she has always left again. Nothing can be done with her; she is so low and so hard.” But the lady said, “She must come in.” The matron then said, “We have been waiting for you. Everyone has gathered, and you have only an hour for your talk.” The lady replied, “No, this matters more.” She went outside to where the woman was sitting and said, “My sister, what is the matter?” “I’m not your sister,” came the reply. Then the lady laid her hand on her and said, “Yes, I am your sister, and I love you.” And she went on speaking like that until the poor woman’s heart was touched. The conversation went on for some time, and the people inside waited patiently. At last the lady brought the woman into the room. There she was, the poor, wretched, degraded creature, full of shame. She would not sit on a chair, but sat on a stool beside the speaker’s seat, and the lady let her lean against her, with her arms around the poor woman’s neck, while she spoke to the gathered people. And that love touched the woman’s heart. She had found someone who truly loved her, and that love opened the way to the love of Jesus. Praise God! there is love on earth in the hearts of God’s children — but oh, that there were more! O God, baptise our ministers with a tender love — and our missionaries, our Bible readers, our workers, and our young men’s and young women’s associations. Oh, that God would begin with us now and baptise us with heavenly love! Love Inspires Intercession Once again: only love can fit us for the work of intercession. I have said that love must fit us for our work. Do you know what the hardest and most important work is that has to be done for this sinful world? It is the work of intercession — going to God and taking time to lay hold of Him. A man may be an earnest Christian, an earnest minister; he may do much good. But how often, sadly, he has to confess that he knows very little of what it means to wait in God’s presence. May God give us the great gift of an intercessory spirit, a spirit of prayer and supplication! I ask you in the name of Jesus not to let a single day go by without praying for all the saints, for all God’s people. I find there are Christians who think little of that. I find prayer unions that pray for their own members, but not for all believers. I beg you, take time to pray for the Church of Christ. It is right to pray for the heathen, as I have already said — God help us to pray for them more. It is right to pray for missionaries, for evangelistic work and for the unconverted. But Paul did not tell people to pray for the heathen or the unconverted. Paul told them to pray for believers. Make this your first prayer every day: “Lord, bless Your saints everywhere.” The condition of Christ’s Church is low beyond words. Plead for God’s people, that He would visit them; plead for one another; plead for all believers who are trying to work for God. Let love fill your heart. Ask Christ to pour it into you afresh every day. Seek to have it brought into you by the Holy Spirit of God: I am set apart for the Holy Spirit, and the fruit of the Spirit is love. God help us to understand it. May God grant that day by day we learn to wait on Him more quietly. Let us not wait on God only for ourselves, or the power to do it will soon be lost. Let us give ourselves to the ministry and the love of intercession, and pray more for God’s people — for God’s people all around us, for the Spirit of love in ourselves and in them, and for the work of God we are part of. The answer will surely come, and our waiting on God will become a source of untold blessing and power. “The fruit of the Spirit is love.” Do you have a lack of love to confess before God? Then confess it, and say before Him, “O Lord, my lack of heart, my lack of love — I confess it.” And then, as you lay that lack at His feet, believe that the blood cleanses you, that Jesus comes in His mighty, cleansing, saving power to set you free, and that He will give His Holy Spirit. “The fruit of the Spirit is love.”

fields.title: Separated to the Holy Spirit
fields.body_html:
SET APART FOR THE HOLY SPIRIT

“Now there were in the church that was at Antioch certain prophets and teachers; as Barnabas, and Simeon that was called Niger, and Lucius of Cyrene, and Manaen . . . and Saul.

“As they ministered to the Lord, and fasted, the Holy Spirit said, Separate me Barnabas and Saul for the work whereunto I have called them.

“And when they had fasted and prayed, and laid their hands on them, they sent them away. So they, being sent forth by the Holy Spirit, departed unto Seleucia” (Acts 13:1-4).

In the story of our text we will find some precious thoughts to guide us about what God wants from us and what God wants to do for us. The great lesson of these verses is this: the Holy Spirit is the director of God’s work on earth. If we are to work rightly for God, and if God is to bless our work, we must make sure we stand in a right relationship to the Holy Spirit. We must give Him, every day, the place of honour that belongs to Him, and see that in all our work — and, more than that, in all our private inner life — the Holy Spirit always has first place. Let me point out some of the precious thoughts our passage suggests.

First of all, we see that God has His own plans for His kingdom.

His church at Antioch had been established. God had particular plans and purposes for Asia and for Europe. He had conceived them; they were His; and He made them known to His servants.

Our great Commander organises every campaign, and His generals and officers do not always know the overall plan. They often receive sealed orders, and they have to wait on Him for whatever orders He gives them. God in heaven has wishes and a will about every piece of work that ought to be done, and about the way it should be done. Blessed is the man who enters into God’s secrets and works under God.

Some years ago, at Wellington in South Africa, where I live, we opened a Mission Institute — a building that is considered large and fine out there. At our opening services the principal said something I have never forgotten:

“Last year we gathered here to lay the foundation stone. What was there to see then? Nothing but rubbish and stones and bricks, the ruins of an old building that had been pulled down. We laid the foundation stone there, and very few people knew what building was going to rise. No one knew it perfectly in every detail except one man, the architect. In his mind it was all clear. As the contractor and the mason and the carpenter came to their work, they took their orders from him; even the humblest labourer had to obey orders; and the structure rose, and this beautiful building has been completed. And in just the same way,” he added, “this building we are opening today is only the laying of the foundation of a work, and only God knows what it will become.”

But God has His workers and His plans clearly mapped out, and our part is to wait for God to tell us as much of His will as we need at each step.

We simply have to be faithful and obedient, carrying out His orders. God has a plan for His Church on earth. But sadly, we too often make our own plan and think we know what ought to be done. We ask God first to bless our feeble efforts, instead of flatly refusing to go unless God goes ahead of us. God has made the plans for the work and the growth of His kingdom. That work has been put into the Holy Spirit’s charge: “The work whereunto I have called them.” So may God help all of us to be afraid of touching “the ark of God” except as the Holy Spirit leads us.

Then the second thought: God is willing and able to show His servants what His will is.

Yes, blessed be God, messages still come down from heaven! Just as we read here what the Holy Spirit said, so the Holy Spirit will still speak to His Church and His people. In these later days He has often done so. He has come to individuals and, by His divine teaching, led them out into fields of work that others could not at first understand or approve, into ways and methods that did not appeal to the majority. The Holy Spirit still teaches His people in our time. Thank God, in our foreign missionary societies, in our home missions and in a thousand forms of work, the guidance of the Holy Spirit is known — but, as I think we are all ready to confess, it is known too little. It is in hearts entirely surrendered to the Lord Jesus — hearts that separate themselves from the world, and even from ordinary religious activities, and give themselves up to intense prayer, looking to their Lord — it is in hearts like these that God’s heavenly will is made known.

You shut out business and company and pleasure and anything that could distract you, because you want to be alone with God. Yet in one way even the material world follows you in there: you have to eat. These men wanted to shut out the influence of the material and the visible, and so they fasted. They ate just enough to meet the needs of nature, and in the intensity of their souls they sought, by fasting before God, to express that they were letting go of everything on earth. Oh, may God give us that intensity of desire, that separation from everything, because we want to wait on God so that the Holy Spirit may reveal His blessed will to us.

“Separate me Barnabas and Saul for the work whereunto I have called them. The work is Mine, and I care for it. I have chosen these men and called them, and I want you, who represent the Church of Christ on earth, to set them apart for Me.”

Look at this heavenly message from both sides. The men were to be set apart to the Holy Spirit, and the Church was to do this work of setting them apart. The Holy Spirit could trust these men to do it in the right spirit. There they were, living in fellowship with heaven, and the Holy Spirit could say to them, “Do the work of setting these men apart.” And these were the men the Holy Spirit had prepared, and He could say of them, “Let them be set apart for Me.”

The question is: what is needed for the power of God to rest on us more mightily, and for the blessing of God to be poured out more abundantly on the poor, wretched people and perishing sinners among whom we work? Oh, the sin is greater than we know! No wonder there is so much weakness and failure in the Church of Christ!

fields.title: Peter's Repentance
fields.body_html:
“And the Lord turned, and looked upon Peter. And Peter remembered the word of the Lord, how he had said unto him, Before the cock crow, thou shalt deny me thrice. And Peter went out, and wept bitterly” (Luke 22:61, 62).

That was the turning point in Peter’s story. Christ had said to him, “Thou canst not follow me now” (John 13:36). Peter was not in a fit state to follow Christ, because he had not been brought to the end of himself. He did not know himself, and so he could not follow Christ. But when he went out and wept bitterly, the great change came. Christ had told him earlier, “When thou art converted, strengthen thy brethren.” This is the point at which Peter was converted from self to Christ.

I thank God for the story of Peter. I don’t know of anyone in the Bible who gives us greater comfort. When we look at his character, so full of failures, and at what Christ made of him by the power of the Holy Spirit, there is hope for every one of us. But remember: before Christ could fill Peter with the Holy Spirit and make a new man of him, Peter had to go out and weep bitterly. He had to be humbled. If we want to understand this, I think there are four points we must look at. First, Peter the devoted disciple of Jesus; next, Peter living the life of self; then Peter in his repentance; and last, what Christ made of Peter by the Holy Spirit.

Peter the Devoted Disciple of Christ

Christ called Peter to leave his nets and follow Him. Peter did so at once, and afterwards he could rightly say to the Lord,

“We have forsaken all and followed thee” (Matt. 19:27).

Peter was a man of absolute surrender; he gave up everything to follow Jesus. Peter was also a man of ready obedience. You remember that Christ said to him, “Launch out into the deep, and let down the net.” Peter the fisherman knew there were no fish there, for they had worked all night and caught nothing. But he said, “At thy word I will let down the net” (Luke 5:4, 5). He submitted to the word of Jesus. He was also a man of great faith. When he saw Christ walking on the sea, he said, “Lord, if it be thou, bid me come unto thee” (Matt. 14:28). And at Christ’s word he stepped out of the boat and walked on the water.

And Peter was a man of spiritual insight. When Christ asked the disciples, “Whom do ye say that I am?” Peter was able to answer, “Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God.” And Christ said, “Blessed art thou, Simon Barjona; for flesh and blood hath not revealed it unto thee, but my Father which is in heaven.” Christ spoke of him as the rock man, and as the one who would have the keys of the kingdom. Peter was a splendid man, a devoted disciple of Jesus. If he were alive today, everyone would call him an advanced Christian. And yet how much was still lacking in Peter!

Peter Living the Life of Self

You remember that just after Christ had said to him, “Flesh and blood hath not revealed it unto thee, but my Father which is in heaven,” Christ began to speak about His sufferings, and Peter dared to say, “Be it far from thee, Lord; this shall not be unto thee.” Then Christ had to say,

“Get thee behind me, Satan; for thou savorest not the things that be of God, but those that be of men” (Matt. 16:22-23).

There was Peter in his self-will, trusting his own wisdom, and actually forbidding Christ to go and die. Where did that come from? Peter trusted in himself and in his own ideas about divine things. Later on we see more than once that the disciples argued about who should be the greatest. Peter was one of them, and he thought he had a right to the very first place. He sought his own honour even above the others. The life of self was strong in Peter. He had left his boats and his nets, but not his old self.

When Christ had spoken to him about His sufferings and said, “Get thee behind me, Satan,” He went on to say, “If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me” (Matt. 16:24). No one can follow Him without doing that. Self must be utterly denied. What does that mean? When Peter denied Christ, we read that he said three times, “I do not know the man.” In other words: “I have nothing to do with Him. He and I are not friends. I deny having any connection with Him.” Christ told Peter that he must deny self like that. Self must be disowned, and every one of its claims rejected. That is the root of true discipleship. But Peter did not understand it and could not obey it. And what happened? When the last night came, Christ said to him,

“Before the cock crow twice thou shalt deny me thrice.”

But how self-confidently Peter answered: “Though all should forsake thee, yet will not I. I am ready to go with thee, to prison and to death” (Mark 14:29; Luke 22:33).

Peter meant it honestly, and he really intended to do it; but Peter did not know himself. He did not believe he was as bad as Jesus said he was.

What are we to do about the flesh, which is completely under the power of sin? Deliverance from that is what we need. Peter did not know it, and that is why, in his self-confidence, he went out and denied his Lord.

Notice how Christ uses that word deny twice. The first time He said to Peter, “Deny self.” The second time He said, “Thou wilt deny me.” It has to be one or the other. We have no other choice: we must either deny self or deny Christ. Two great powers are fighting each other — the self-nature in the power of sin, and Christ in the power of God. One or the other must rule within us.

Eve wanted something for herself, and so our first parents fell into all the misery of sin. We, their children, have inherited a dreadful nature of sin.
