Peter denied his Lord three times, and then the Lord looked at him. That look from Jesus broke Peter’s heart. All at once he saw the terrible sin he had committed, the terrible failure that had come, and the depths he had fallen to — and “Peter went out and wept bitterly.”

Oh, who can say what that repentance must have been like? Through the remaining hours of that night, and the next day, when he saw Christ crucified and buried, and the day after that, the Sabbath — oh, in what hopeless despair and shame he must have spent that day!

“My Lord is gone, my hope is gone, and I denied my Lord. After that life of love, after those three years of blessed fellowship, I denied my Lord. God have mercy on me!”

I don’t think we can grasp how deep the humiliation was that Peter sank into then. But that was the turning point and the change. On the first day of the week Christ appeared to Peter, and in the evening He met him with the others. Later, by the Lake of Galilee, He asked him, “Lovest thou me?” — until Peter was grieved, sensing that the Lord was reminding him that he had denied Him three times. And Peter said, in sorrow but in honesty,

“Lord, thou knowest all things; thou knowest that I love thee” (John 21:17).

Peter Transformed

Now Peter was ready to be delivered from self, and that is my last point. You know that Christ took him, with the others, to the footstool of the throne and told them to wait there. Then, on the day of Pentecost, the Holy Spirit came, and Peter was a changed man. I don’t want you to think only of the change you can see in Peter — the boldness, the power, the insight into the Scriptures, and the blessing with which he preached that day. Thank God for all that. But Peter received something deeper and better. Peter’s whole nature was changed. The work Christ began in Peter when He looked at him was completed when Peter was filled with the Holy Spirit.

If you want to see that, read the First Epistle of Peter. You know where Peter’s failings lay. When he said to Christ, in effect, “You can never suffer; it cannot be,” he showed that he had no idea what it meant to pass through death into life. Christ said, “Deny thyself,” and in spite of that, Peter denied his Lord. When Christ warned him, “Thou shalt deny me,” and he insisted he never would, Peter showed how little he understood what was in himself. But when I read his epistle and hear him say, “If ye be reproached for the name of Christ, happy are ye, for the Spirit of God and of glory resteth upon you” (1 Pet. 4:14), I say that this is not the old Peter. This is the very Spirit of Christ breathing and speaking in him.

I read again how he says, “Hereunto ye are called, to suffer, even as Christ suffered” (1 Pet. 2:21). I understand what a change had come over Peter. Instead of denying Christ, he found joy and delight in having self denied and crucified and handed over to death. That is why we read in Acts that when he was called before the Council, he could boldly say, “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29), and that he could go back with the other disciples rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer for Christ’s name.

You remember his self-exaltation; but now he has discovered that “the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit is in the sight of God of great price.” He also tells us to be “subject one to another, and be clothed with humility” (1 Pet. 5:5).

Dear friend, I urge you, look at Peter, utterly changed. The self-pleasing, self-trusting, self-seeking Peter, full of sin, always getting into trouble, foolish and impulsive, is now filled with the Spirit and the life of Jesus. Christ had done it for him by the Holy Spirit.

And now, what is my purpose in pointing so briefly to the story of Peter? His story must become the story of every believer who is really to be made a blessing by God. His story is a prophecy of what everyone can receive from God in heaven.

Let us now take a quick look at what these lessons teach us.

The first lesson is this: you may be a very earnest, godly, devoted believer in whom the power of the flesh is still very strong.

That is a very solemn truth. Before Peter denied Christ, he had cast out demons and healed the sick; and yet the flesh had power in him, and the flesh had room in him. Oh, beloved, we must realise that it is precisely because there is so much of this self-life in us that the power of God cannot work in us as mightily as God wants it to. Do you realise that the great God is longing to double His blessing — to give tenfold blessing — through us? But something is hindering Him, and that something is nothing other than the self-life. We talk about Peter’s pride, Peter’s impulsiveness, Peter’s self-confidence. It was all rooted in that one word, self. Christ had said, “Deny self,” and Peter had never understood it and never obeyed it; and every failing came out of that.

What a solemn thought, and what an urgent reason for us to cry out, “O God, show us this, so that none of us may go on living the self-life!” It has happened to many who had been Christians for years, perhaps even in a prominent position: God found them out and taught them to find themselves out, and they became utterly ashamed and fell down broken before God. Oh, the bitter shame and sorrow and pain and agony they went through, until at last they found that there was deliverance! Peter went out and wept bitterly — and there may be many godly people in whom the power of the flesh still rules.

My second lesson is this: it is the work of our blessed Lord Jesus to reveal the power of self.

How did Peter — the carnal Peter, the self-willed Peter, Peter with his strong self-love — ever become a man of Pentecost and the writer of his epistles? It was because Christ had him in His care. Christ watched over him, and Christ taught him and blessed him. The warnings Christ had given him were part of the training; and last of all came that look of love. In His suffering Christ did not forget him, but turned around and looked at him, and “Peter went out and wept bitterly.” And the Christ who led Peter to Pentecost is waiting today to take charge of every heart that is willing to surrender itself to Him.

Aren’t some of you saying, “Ah! that is my trouble. It is always the self-life — self-comfort, self-consciousness, self-pleasing and self-will. How am I to get rid of it?”

My answer is: Christ Jesus can rid you of it. No one but Christ Jesus can give deliverance from the power of self. And what does He ask you to do? He asks you to humble yourself before Him.

fields.title: Impossible with Man, Possible with God
fields.body_html:
“And he said, The things which are impossible with men are possible with God” (Luke 18:27).

Christ had said to the rich young ruler, “Sell all that thou hast . . . and come, follow me.” The young man went away sad. Then Christ turned to the disciples and said, “How hardly shall they that have riches enter into the kingdom of God!” The disciples, we read, were greatly astonished, and answered, “If it is so hard to enter the kingdom, who then can be saved?” And Christ gave this blessed answer:

“The things which are impossible with men are possible with God.”

The text contains two thoughts. The first is that in religion — in the matter of salvation and of following Christ in a holy life — it is impossible for man to do it. And alongside it is the second: what is impossible with man is possible with God.

These two thoughts mark the two great lessons we have to learn in the religious life. It often takes a long time to learn the first lesson: that in religion man can do nothing, that salvation is impossible for man. And often a person learns that, yet never learns the second lesson — that what has been impossible for him is possible with God. Blessed is the one who learns both lessons! Learning them marks the stages of the Christian life.

Man Cannot

The first stage is when a person tries his very best and fails, tries to do better and fails again, tries much harder and still always fails. And yet very often, even then, he does not learn the lesson: with man it is impossible to serve God and Christ. Peter spent three years in Christ’s school and never learned that it is impossible until he had denied his Lord and gone out and wept bitterly. Then he learned it.

Look for a moment at someone who is learning this lesson. At first he fights against it. Then he submits to it, but reluctantly and in despair. At last he accepts it willingly and rejoices in it. At the beginning of the Christian life the young convert has no idea of this truth. He has been converted; he has the joy of the Lord in his heart; he begins to run the race and fight the battle. He is sure he can win, because he is earnest and honest, and God will help him. Yet somehow, very soon, he fails where he never expected to, and sin gets the better of him. He is disappointed, but he thinks, “I wasn’t watchful enough. I didn’t make my resolutions strong enough.” So he makes his vows again, and prays again, and still he fails. He thought, “Am I not a regenerate man? Don’t I have the life of God within me?” And again he thinks, “Yes — and I have Christ to help me. I can live the holy life.”

Later he reaches a different state of mind. He begins to see that such a life is impossible, but he does not accept it. Multitudes of Christians come to this point — “I cannot” — and then conclude that God never expected them to do what they cannot do. If you tell them that God does expect it, it seems a mystery to them. A great many Christians are living a low life, a life of failure and sin, instead of rest and victory, because they began to see, “I cannot; it is impossible.” Yet they do not understand it fully, and so, with the feeling “I cannot” hanging over them, they give way to despair. They will do their best, but they never expect to get very far.

But God leads His children on to a third stage. Now a person takes it is impossible in its full truth, and yet at the same time says, “I must do it, and I will do it. It is impossible for man, and yet I must do it.” The renewed will begins to use all its strength, and with intense longing and prayer begins to cry out to God, “Lord, what does this mean? How am I to be set free from the power of sin?”

This is the condition of the regenerate man in Romans 7. There you find the Christian trying his very utmost to live a holy life. God’s law has been revealed to him as reaching down to the deepest desires of the heart, and he can boldly say:

“I delight in the law of God after the inward man. To will what is good is present with me. My heart loves the law of God, and my will has chosen that law.”

Can someone like that fail, with his heart full of delight in God’s law and his will set on doing what is right? Yes. That is what Romans 7 teaches us. Something more is needed. It is not enough that I delight in the law of God in my inner being and will what God wills; I need divine omnipotence to work it out in me. And that is what the apostle Paul teaches in Philippians 2:13:

“It is God which worketh in you, both to will and to do.”

Notice the contrast. In Romans 7 the regenerate man says, “To will is present with me, but to do — I find I cannot do it. I will, but I cannot carry it out.” But in Philippians 2 you have someone who has been led further on — someone who understands that when God has produced the renewed will, God will give the power to accomplish what that will desires. Let us take this as the first great lesson of the spiritual life: “It is impossible for me, my God. Let there be an end of the flesh and all its powers, an end of self; and let my glory be to be helpless.”

Praise God for the divine teaching that makes us helpless!

When you thought about absolute surrender to God, weren’t you brought to the end of yourself? Didn’t you feel that you could not see how you could actually live as someone absolutely surrendered to God every moment of the day — at your table, in your house, in your business, in the middle of trials and temptations? I beg you, learn the lesson now. If you felt you could not do it, you are on the right road, so long as you let yourself be led. Accept that position and hold to it before God: “O God, my heart’s desire and delight is absolute surrender, but I cannot carry it out. It is impossible for me to live that life. It is beyond me.” Fall down before Him and learn that when you are utterly helpless, God will come and work in you not only to will, but also to do.

God Can

Now comes the second lesson: “The things which are impossible with men are possible with God.”

I said a little while ago that many people have learned the lesson it is impossible with men, and then give up in helpless despair and live a wretched Christian life without joy or strength or victory. Why? Because they do not humble themselves to learn the other lesson: with God all things are possible.

Your religious life is meant to be, every day, a proof that God does impossible things. Your religious life is meant to be a series of impossibilities made possible and real by God’s almighty power. That is what the Christian needs. He worships an almighty God, and he must come to understand that he does not need a little of God’s power. He needs — I say it reverently — the whole of God’s omnipotence to keep him right and to live like a Christian.

The whole of Christianity is a work of God’s omnipotence. Look at the birth of Christ Jesus. That was a miracle of divine power, and it was said to Mary, “With God nothing shall be impossible.” It was the omnipotence of God. Look at Christ’s resurrection. We are taught that it was according to the exceeding greatness of His mighty power that God raised Christ from the dead.

Every tree must grow from the root it springs from. An oak tree three hundred years old has grown all that time from the one root where it began. Christianity began in the omnipotence of God, and in every soul it must continue in that omnipotence. All the possibilities of the higher Christian life spring from a fresh grasp of Christ’s power to work all of God’s will in us.

I want to call you now to come and worship an almighty God. Have you learned to do it? Have you learned to deal so closely with an almighty God that you know omnipotence is at work in you? Outwardly there is often very little sign of it. The apostle Paul said, “I was with you in weakness and in fear and in much trembling, and . . . my preaching was . . . in demonstration of the Spirit and of power.” On the human side there was weakness; on the divine side there was divine omnipotence. That is true of every godly life. If only we would learn that lesson better and give ourselves to it in wholehearted, undivided surrender, we would learn what blessedness there is in living every hour and every moment with an almighty God. Have you ever studied God’s omnipotence as it is shown in the Bible? You know that it was God’s omnipotence that created the world, created light out of darkness, and created man. But have you studied God’s omnipotence in the works of redemption?

Look at Abraham. When God called him to be the father of the people from whom Christ was to be born, God said to him, “I am God Almighty, walk before me and be thou perfect.” And God trained Abraham to trust Him as the Almighty One. Whether it was going out to a land he did not know; or his faith as a pilgrim among thousands of Canaanites, when his faith said, “This is my land”; or his faith in waiting twenty-five years for a son in his old age, against all hope; or his faith that God would raise Isaac from the dead on Mount Moriah when he was about to sacrifice him — Abraham believed God. fields.title: O Wretched Man that I am!
fields.body_html:
“O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death? I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Romans 7:24, 25).

You know what a wonderful place this text holds in the wonderful epistle to the Romans. It stands at the end of the seventh chapter as the gateway into the eighth. In the first sixteen verses of the eighth chapter the name of the Holy Spirit appears sixteen times; there you have the description and the promise of the life a child of God can live in the power of the Holy Spirit. It begins in the second verse: “The law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus hath made me free from the law of sin and death” (Rom. 8:2). From there Paul goes on to speak of the great privileges of the child of God, who is to be led by the Spirit of God. And the gateway into all of this is the twenty-fourth verse of the seventh chapter:

“O wretched man that I am!”

These are the words of a man who has come to the end of himself. In the verses before, he has described how he struggled and wrestled in his own strength to obey God’s holy law, and failed. But now he finds the true answer to his own question, and cries out, “I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord.” From there he goes on to speak of the deliverance he has found.

From these words I want to describe the path by which a person can be led out of the spirit of bondage into the spirit of liberty. You know how plainly it is said, “Ye have not received the spirit of bondage again to fear.” We are constantly warned that this is the great danger of the Christian life — slipping back into bondage. So I want to describe the path by which a person can get out of bondage into the glorious liberty of the children of God. Or rather, I want to describe the man himself.

First, these words are the language of a regenerate man; second, of a powerless man; third, of a wretched man; and fourth, of a man on the very edge of complete liberty.

The Regenerate Man

From the fourteenth verse of the chapter to the twenty-third there is plenty of evidence of regeneration. “It is no more I that do it, but sin that dwelleth in me” (Rom. 7:17): that is the language of a regenerate man — a man who knows that his heart and nature have been renewed, and that sin is now a power in him that is not his true self. “I delight in the law of the Lord after the inward man” (Rom. 7:22): that, again, is the language of a regenerate man. When he does evil he dares to say, “It is no more I that do it, but sin that dwelleth in me.” It is very important to understand this.

In the first two great sections of the epistle, Paul deals with justification and sanctification. When he deals with justification, he lays the foundation of the doctrine in his teaching about sin — not in the singular, sin, but in the plural, sins, meaning actual wrongdoings. In the second half of the fifth chapter he begins to deal with sin not as actual wrongdoing but as a power. Just imagine what a loss it would have been to us if we did not have this second half of the seventh chapter of Romans — if Paul had left out of his teaching this vital question of sin in the believer. We would have missed the answer we all want about sin in the believer. And what is the answer? The regenerate man is one whose will has been renewed, and who can say, “I delight in the law of God after the inward man.”

The Powerless Man

Here is the great mistake many Christians make: they think that once there is a renewed will, that is enough. But it is not. This regenerate man tells us, “I will to do what is good, but the power to perform I find not.” How often people tell us that if you set yourself to it with determination, you can do whatever you will! But this man was as determined as anyone can be, and still he confessed, “To will is present with me; but how to perform that which is good, I find not” (Rom. 7:18).

But you ask, “Why would God make a regenerate man say such a thing — a man with a right will, with a heart that longs to do good and longs to do its very utmost to love God?”

Let us look at that question. What has God given us our will for? Did the angels who fell have, in their own will, the strength to stand? Certainly not. A creature’s will is nothing but an empty vessel in which God’s power is to be displayed. The creature must look to God for everything it is to be. You find it in the second chapter of Philippians, and you find it here too: God’s work is to work in us both to will and to do of His good pleasure. Yet here is a man who seems to be saying, “God has not worked to do in me.” But we are taught that God works both to will and to do. How is this apparent contradiction to be resolved?

You will find that in this passage (Rom. 7:6-25) the name of the Holy Spirit does not appear once, and neither does the name of Christ. The man is wrestling and struggling to fulfil God’s law. Instead of the Holy Spirit and Christ, the law is mentioned nearly twenty times. This chapter shows a believer doing his very best to obey God’s law with his regenerate will. And not only that: you will find that the little words I, me, my occur more than forty times. It is the regenerate I, in its powerlessness, trying to obey the law without being filled with the Spirit. This is the experience of almost every saint. After conversion a person begins to do his best, and he fails. But if we are brought into the full light, we need fail no longer. In fact, we need not fail at all if we received the Spirit in His fullness at conversion.

God allows that failure so that the regenerate man may be taught his own utter powerlessness. It is in the course of this struggle that the sense of our utter sinfulness comes to us. This is God’s way of dealing with us. He lets the man strive to fulfil the law so that, as he strives and wrestles, he may be brought to this: “I am a regenerate child of God, but I am utterly helpless to obey His law.” Look at the strong words used throughout the chapter to describe this condition: “I am carnal, sold under sin” (Rom. 7:14); “I see another law in my members bringing me into captivity” (Rom. 7:23); and last of all, “O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death?” (Rom. 7:24). This believer, bowing here in deep sorrow for sin, is utterly unable to obey the law of God.

The Wretched Man

The man who makes this confession is not only regenerate and powerless; he is also wretched. He is utterly unhappy and miserable. And what makes him so utterly miserable? It is that God has given him a nature that loves Him. He is deeply wretched because he feels he is not obeying his God. With a broken heart he says, “It is not I who do it, but I am under the dreadful power of sin, which is holding me down. It is I, and yet not I. Alas, alas! it is myself, so tightly am I bound up with it, and so closely is it woven into my very nature.” Blessed be God when a man learns to say from the depths of his heart, “O wretched man that I am!” He is on the way to the eighth chapter of Romans.

Many people make this confession a pillow for sin. They say that if Paul had to confess his weakness and helplessness like this, who are they to try to do better? And so the call to holiness is quietly set aside. If only every one of us had learned to say these words in the very spirit in which they are written here! When we hear sin spoken of as the abominable thing God hates, don’t many of us flinch at the word? If only all the Christians who go on sinning and sinning would take this verse to heart! If you ever say a sharp word, say, “O wretched man that I am!” And every time you lose your temper, kneel down and understand that God never meant this to be the condition His child should stay in. If only we would take this word into our daily life and say it every time our pride is touched, every time we say sharp things, every time we sin against the Lord God and against the Lord Jesus Christ in His humility, His obedience and His self-sacrifice! If only you could forget everything else and cry out, “O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death?”

Why should you say this whenever you sin? Because it is when a person is brought to this confession that deliverance is near.

And remember, it was not only the sense of being powerless and held captive that made him wretched. Above all, it was the sense of sinning against his God. The law was doing its work, making sin exceedingly sinful in his eyes. All their lack of joy in the Holy Spirit, and their lack of the liberty He gives, is due simply to the flesh. The Spirit is within them, but the flesh rules their life. What they need is to be led by the Spirit of God. If only I could make every one of God’s children realise what it means that the everlasting God has given His dear Son, Christ Jesus, to watch over you every day; that what you have to do is trust; and that the Holy Spirit’s work is to enable you every moment to remember Jesus and to trust Him! The Spirit has come to keep the link with Him unbroken every moment. Praise God for the Holy Spirit! We are so used to thinking of the Holy Spirit as a luxury, for special occasions or for special ministers and people. But the Holy Spirit is necessary for every believer, every moment of the day. Praise God that you have Him, and that He gives you the full experience of deliverance in Christ as He sets you free from the power of sin.

“O God, must I go on sinning like this for ever? Who shall deliver me, O wretched man that I am! from the body of this death?”

Are you ready to sink down before God with that cry, and to seek the power of Jesus to live and work in you? Are you ready to say, “I thank God through Jesus Christ”?

What good does it do us to go to church or attend conventions, to study our Bibles and pray, unless our lives are filled with the Holy Spirit? That is what God wants, and nothing else will enable us to live a life of power and peace. You know that when a minister or parent is teaching the catechism and asks a question, an answer is expected. Instead of answering, they stay silent. Instead of saying, “I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord,” they go on repeating the question for ever without the answer. Say, “I, a wretched man, thank God through Jesus Christ. Even though I don’t see it all, I am going to praise God.”

fields.title: Having Begun in the Spirit
fields.body_html:
The words I want to speak to you from are found in the epistle to the Galatians, chapter three, verse three. Let us read the second verse as well: “This only would I learn of you, Received ye the Spirit by the works of the law, or by the hearing of faith? Are ye so foolish?” And then comes my text: “Having begun in the Spirit, are ye now made perfect by the flesh?”

When we speak of the quickening or deepening or strengthening of the spiritual life, we are thinking of something that is weak and wrong and sinful. And it is a great thing to take our place before God with the confession:

“Oh, God, our spiritual life is not what it should be!”

May God work that in your heart, reader.

As we look around at the Church, we see so many signs of weakness and failure, of sin and shortcoming, that we are forced to ask: Why is this? Does the Church of Christ have to live in such a low condition? Or is it actually possible for God’s people to live always in the joy and strength of their God?

Every believing heart must answer: it is possible.

Then comes the great question: why is it — how are we to explain it — that God’s Church as a whole is so weak, and that the great majority of Christians are not living up to their privileges? There must be a reason. Has God not given Christ, His almighty Son, to be the Keeper of every believer, to make Christ an ever-present reality, and to give and pass on to us all that we have in Christ? God has given His Son, and God has given His Spirit. So why do believers not live up to their privileges?

In more than one of the epistles we find a very solemn answer to that question. There are epistles, such as First Thessalonians, in which Paul writes to the Christians, in effect, “I want you to grow, to abound, to increase more and more.” They were young, and there were things lacking in their faith, but on the whole their condition was satisfactory and gave him great joy. Again and again he writes, “I pray God that you may abound more and more; I write to you to increase more and more” (1 Thes. 4:1,10). But in other epistles he takes a very different tone — especially in the epistles to the Corinthians and the Galatians. There he tells them in many different ways what the one reason was why they were not living as Christians ought to live: many of them were under the power of the flesh. My text is one example. He reminds them that it was through the preaching of faith that they had received the Holy Spirit. He had preached Christ to them; they had accepted that Christ and had received the Holy Spirit in power. But what happened? Having begun in the Spirit, they tried to complete in the flesh, by their own effort, the work the Spirit had begun. We find the same teaching in the epistle to the Corinthians.

Here, then, is a solemn discovery of what the Church of Christ chiefly lacks. God has called the Church of Christ to live in the power of the Holy Spirit, and for the most part the Church is living in the power of human flesh — of will and energy and effort apart from the Spirit of God. I have no doubt that is the case with many individual believers. And oh, if God will use me to bring you a message from Him, my one message will be this: “If the Church will return to acknowledging that the Holy Spirit is her strength and her help, and if the Church will return to giving up everything and waiting on God to be filled with the Spirit, her days of beauty and gladness will return, and we will see the glory of God revealed among us.” And this is my message to every individual believer: “Nothing will help you unless you come to understand that you must live every day under the power of the Holy Spirit.”

God wants you to be a living vessel in which the power of the Spirit is displayed every hour and every moment of your life, and God will enable you to be that.

So let us try to learn some very simple lessons that this word to the Galatians teaches us. It shows us (1) that the Christian life begins with receiving the Holy Spirit. It shows us (2) how great the danger is of forgetting that we are to live by the Spirit and not after the flesh. It shows us (3) what the fruits and the evidences are of seeking perfection in the flesh. And then it points us to (4) the way of deliverance from this condition.

Receiving the Holy Spirit

First of all, Paul says, “Having begun in the Spirit.” Remember, the apostle did not only preach justification by faith; he preached something more. He preached this — and the epistle is full of it — that justified people cannot live except by the Holy Spirit, and that God therefore gives the Holy Spirit to every justified person to seal him. More than once the apostle says to them, in effect:

“How did you receive the Holy Spirit? Was it by the preaching of the law, or by the preaching of faith?”

He could point back to the time when there had been a mighty revival under his teaching. The power of God had been displayed, and the Galatians were bound to admit:

“Yes, we have received the Holy Spirit. When we accepted Christ by faith, by faith we received the Holy Spirit.”

Now, I fear there are many Christians who hardly know that when they believed, they received the Holy Spirit. A great many Christians can say, “I received pardon, and I received peace.” But if you asked them, “Have you received the Holy Spirit?” they would hesitate. Many of them, if they said yes at all, would say it hesitantly, and would tell you they hardly knew what it meant, since then, to walk in the power of the Holy Spirit. Let us try to lay hold of this great truth: the true Christian life begins with receiving the Holy Spirit. And the work of every Christian minister is the same as Paul’s work — to remind his people that they have received the Holy Spirit and must live under His guidance and in His power.

If those Galatians, who received the Holy Spirit in power, were tempted to go astray through that terrible danger of completing in the flesh what had been begun in the Spirit, how much greater is the danger for Christians who hardly know they have received the Holy Spirit — or who, if they believe it as a doctrine, hardly ever think about it and hardly ever praise God for it!

Neglecting the Holy Spirit

But now look, in the second place, at the great danger.

You all know what shunting is on a railway. A locomotive and its train may be running in a certain direction. At some point the points may not be properly set, and without anyone noticing, the train is shunted off to the right or the left. If that happens on a dark night, say, the train heads the wrong way, and the passengers may not know it until they have gone some distance.

In just the same way, God gives Christians the Holy Spirit with this intention: that every day of their whole life should be lived in the power of the Spirit. No one can live a godly life for a single hour except by the power of the Holy Spirit. He may live a proper, consistent life, as people call it — a blameless life, a life of virtue and diligent service. But to live a life that pleases God, enjoying God’s salvation and God’s love, living and walking in the power of the new life — he cannot do that unless he is guided by the Holy Spirit every day and every hour.

But now listen to the danger. The Galatians received the Holy Spirit, but they tried to complete in the flesh what had been begun by the Spirit. How? They fell back under the influence of Judaizing teachers who told them they had to be circumcised. They began to look for their religion in outward observances. That is why Paul says of those teachers who had them circumcised that “they sought to glory in their flesh” (Gal. 6:13).

You sometimes hear the expression religious flesh. What does it mean? It is simply a way of putting this thought into words: my human nature, my human will and my human effort can be very active in religion. After being converted, and after receiving the Holy Spirit, I may start trying to serve God in my own strength.

I may be very diligent and do a great deal, and yet all along it may be more the work of human flesh than of God’s Spirit. What a solemn thought — that a person can, without noticing it, be shunted off the line of the Holy Spirit onto the line of the flesh; that he can be extremely diligent and make great sacrifices, and yet it is all in the power of the human will! Ah, the great thing for us to ask of God as we examine ourselves is that He would show us whether our religious life is lived more in the power of the flesh than in the power of the Holy Spirit. A man may be a preacher and work very diligently in his ministry; a man may be a Christian worker, and others may say of him that he makes great sacrifices — and yet you can sense that something is missing. You feel he is not a spiritual man; there is nothing spiritual about his life. How many Christians there are of whom no one would ever think of saying, “What a spiritual man he is!” Ah, there is the weakness of the Church of Christ. It all comes down to that one word — flesh.

Now, the flesh can show itself in many ways. It can show itself as fleshly wisdom. My mind may be very active about religion. I may preach or write or think or meditate, and enjoy being busy with the things of God’s Book and God’s kingdom — and yet the power of the Holy Spirit may be noticeably absent. Look at the preaching throughout the Church of Christ and ask why, sadly, there is so little converting power in the preaching of the Word; why there is so much work and often so little result for eternity; why the Word has so little power to build believers up in holiness and consecration. I fear the answer will be: it is the absence of the power of the Holy Spirit. And why is that? There can be no other reason than this: the flesh and human energy have taken the place that belongs to the Holy Spirit. That was true of the Galatians, and it was true of the Corinthians. You know Paul said to them, “I cannot speak to you as to spiritual men; you ought to be spiritual men, but you are carnal.” And you know how often in his epistles he had to rebuke and condemn them for quarrelling and divisions.

Lacking the Fruit of the Holy Spirit

A third thought: what are the evidences or signs that a church like the Galatians, or an individual Christian, is serving God in the power of the flesh — is completing in the flesh what was begun in the Spirit?

The answer is very easy. Religious self-effort always ends in sinful flesh. What was the condition of those Galatians? They were striving to be justified by the works of the law — and yet they were quarrelling and in danger of devouring one another. Count the expressions the apostle uses to describe their lack of love, and you will find more than twelve: envy, jealousy, bitterness, strife and all sorts of others. Read what he says about it in the fourth and fifth chapters. You see how they tried to serve God in their own strength and failed completely. All this religious effort ended in failure. The power of sin and the sinful flesh got the better of them, and their whole condition was about as sad as could be imagined.

This comes to us with a solemnity beyond words. Everywhere in the Christian Church there is a complaint about the lack of a high standard of integrity and godliness, even among professing members of Christian churches. Think of the life God has called His children to, and which He enables them to live by the Holy Spirit. Then we are forced to ask, “Where are the marks of the presence of the Spirit of the Lamb of God?” Missing — sadly missing!

Many people speak of these things as though they were the natural result of our weakness and could not really be helped. Many speak of them as sins, but have given up hope of conquering them. Many speak of these things in the church around them and see not the slightest prospect of anything ever changing. fields.title: Kept by the Power of God
fields.body_html:
The words I am speaking from are found in 1 Peter 1:5. Verses three, four and five read: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, which . . . hath begotten us again unto a lively hope by the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, to an inheritance incorruptible . . . reserved in heaven for you, who are kept by the power of God through faith unto salvation.” The words of my text are: “Kept by the power of God through faith.”

Here we have two wonderful, blessed truths about the keeping by which a believer is kept for salvation. One truth is, kept by the power of God; the other is, kept through faith. We should look at both sides: at God’s side, His almighty power offered to us to be our Keeper every moment of the day; and at the human side, where we have nothing to do but, in faith, to let God do His work of keeping. We have been born again to an inheritance kept in heaven for us, and here on earth we are kept by the power of God. So we see there is a double keeping — the inheritance kept for me in heaven, and I on earth kept for the inheritance there.

Now, about the first part of this keeping there is no doubt and no question. God keeps the inheritance in heaven wonderfully and perfectly, and it is waiting there in safety. And the same God keeps me for the inheritance. That is what I want to understand.

You know it would be very foolish for a father to go to great trouble to secure an inheritance for his children and keep it for them, if he does not keep them for it. Imagine a man who spends all his time and makes every sacrifice to pile up money. As he gains his tens of thousands, you ask him why he sacrifices himself like this, and he answers, “I want to leave my children a large inheritance, and I am keeping it for them.” Then you hear that the man takes no trouble to educate his children; that he lets them run wild in the streets and go on in paths of sin and ignorance and folly. What would you think of him? Wouldn’t you say, “Poor man! He is keeping an inheritance for his children, but he is not keeping or preparing his children for the inheritance”? And so many Christians think, “My God is keeping the inheritance for me,” but they cannot believe, “My God is keeping me for that inheritance.” Yet it is the same power, the same love, the same God doing the double work.

Now I want to speak about a work God does on us — keeping us for the inheritance. I have already said that we have two very simple truths: the divine side — we are kept by the power of God; and the human side — we are kept through faith.

Kept by the Power of God

Look at the divine side: Christians are kept by the power of God.

Keeping Includes All

Think, first of all, that this keeping includes everything.

What is kept? You are kept. How much of you? Your whole being. Does God keep one part of you and not another? No. Some people have the idea that this is a kind of vague, general keeping — that God will keep them in such a way that when they die they will get to heaven. But they do not apply that word kept to everything in their being and nature. And yet that is what God wants.

I have a watch here. Suppose I had borrowed this watch from a friend, and he said to me,

“When you go to Europe, I’ll let you take it with you, but mind you keep it safe and bring it back.”

And suppose I damaged the watch — broke the hands, spoiled the face, and ruined some of the wheels and springs — and took it back in that condition and handed it to my friend. He would say,

“Ah, but I gave you that watch on condition that you would keep it.”

“Haven’t I kept it? There’s the watch.”

“But I didn’t want you to keep it in that general way, and bring me back only the case of the watch, or what’s left of it. I expected you to keep every part of it.”

In the same way, God does not want to keep us in a general way, so that at the end, somehow or other, we are saved as by fire and just scrape into heaven. No — God’s keeping power and love apply to every detail of our being.

Some people think God will keep them in spiritual things but not in everyday, material things. That, they say, lies outside His sphere. Now, God sends you to work in the world, but He did not say, “I must now leave you to go and earn your own money and make your own living.” He knows you are not able to keep yourself. God says, “My child, there is no work you have to do, no business you are involved in, not a cent you have to spend, that I, your Father, will not take into My keeping.” God cares not only for the spiritual but for the material as well. Many people must spend the greater part of their lives — sometimes eight or nine or ten hours a day — among the temptations and distractions of business. But God will care for you there. God’s keeping includes everything.

Other people think, “Ah, in times of trial God keeps me, but in times of prosperity I don’t need His keeping; then I forget Him and let Him go.” Others think the very opposite: “In times of prosperity, when things are smooth and quiet, I can cling to God. But when heavy trials come, somehow my will rebels, and God doesn’t keep me then.”

I bring you the message that in prosperity as in adversity, in sunshine as in darkness, your God is ready to keep you all the time.

Then again, there are others who think of this keeping like this: “God will keep me from doing very great wickedness, but there are small sins I can’t expect God to keep me from. There is the sin of temper. I can’t expect God to conquer that.”

When you hear of someone who has been tempted and has gone astray, or fallen into drunkenness or murder, you thank God for His keeping power.

“I might have done the same as that man,” you say, “if God had not kept me.” And you believe He kept you from drunkenness and murder.

So why don’t you believe that God can keep you from outbursts of temper? You thought this was less important. You forgot that the great commandment of the New Testament is “Love one another as I have loved you” (John 13:34). When your temper and hasty judgments and sharp words came out, you sinned against the highest law — the law of God’s love. And yet you say, “God will not, God cannot” — no, you won’t say “God cannot,” but you say, “God doesn’t keep me from that.” Perhaps you say, “He can; but there is something in me that can never reach it, and God doesn’t take it away.”

I want to ask you: can believers live a holier life than is generally lived? Can believers experience God’s keeping power all day long, keeping them from sin? Can believers be kept in fellowship with God? I bring you a message from the Word of God in these words: kept by the power of God. There is no qualifying clause attached. It means that if you will entrust yourself entirely and absolutely to the omnipotence of God, He will delight to keep you.

Some people think they can never reach the point where every word from their mouth is for the glory of God. But it is what God wants of them; it is what God expects of them. God is willing to set a guard at the door of their mouth — and if God will do that, can He not keep their tongue and their lips? He can, and that is what God is going to do for those who trust Him. God’s keeping includes everything. Let everyone who longs to live a holy life think through all their needs, all their weaknesses, all their shortcomings and all their sins, and ask deliberately, “Is there any sin my God cannot keep me from?” And the heart will have to answer, “No; God can keep me from every sin.”

Keeping Requires Power

Second, if you want to understand this keeping, remember that it is not only a keeping that includes everything; it is an almighty keeping.

I want to have that truth burned into my soul. I want to worship God until my whole heart is filled with the thought of His omnipotence. God is almighty, and the Almighty God offers Himself to work in my heart and do the work of keeping me. I want to be joined to Omnipotence — or rather, joined to the Omnipotent One, the living God — and to have my place in the hollow of His hand. You read the Psalms and think of the wonderful thoughts in so many of David’s expressions — for instance, when he speaks of God as our God, our Fortress, our Refuge, our strong Tower, our Strength and our Salvation. David had wonderful views of how the everlasting God is Himself the hiding place of the believing soul; of how He takes the believer and keeps him in the very hollow of His hand, in the secret of His pavilion, under the shadow of His wings, under His very feathers. And that is where David lived. And oh, we who are children of Pentecost, we who have known Christ and His blood and the Holy Spirit sent down from heaven — why do we know so little of what it means to walk, trembling, step by step, with the Almighty God as our Keeper?

Have you ever thought that in every working of grace in your heart, the whole omnipotence of God is engaged to bless you? When I go to a man and he gives me a gift of money, I take it and go away with it. He has given me something of his, and the rest he keeps for himself. But that is not how it is with the power of God. God cannot part with any of His own power. So I can experience God’s power and goodness only as far as I am in contact and fellowship with Him Himself. And when I come into contact and fellowship with Him, I come into contact and fellowship with the whole omnipotence of God, and I have God’s omnipotence to help me every day.

Perhaps a son has a very rich father, and as the son is about to start in business, the father says, “You can have as much money as you want for your venture.” Everything the father has is at the son’s disposal. That is how it is with God, your Almighty God. You can hardly take it in; you feel like such a little worm. His omnipotence needed to keep a little worm! Yes — His omnipotence is needed to keep every little worm that lives in the dust, and to keep the universe as well; and so His omnipotence is needed far more to keep your soul and mine from the power of sin.

Oh, if you want to grow in grace, do learn to begin here. In all your judgments and meditations, your thoughts and deeds, your questions and studies and prayers, learn to be kept by your Almighty God. What will Almighty God not do for the child who trusts Him? The Bible says, “Above all that we can ask or think” (Eph. 3:20). It is Omnipotence you must learn to know and trust, and then you will live as a Christian ought to live. How little we have learned to study God, and to understand that a godly life is a life full of God — a life that loves God and waits on Him and trusts Him and lets Him bless it! We cannot do God’s will except by God’s power. God gives us our first experience of His power to make us long for more, and to come and claim all He can do. God help us to trust Him every day.

Keeping Is Continuous

Another thought: this keeping is not only all-inclusive and almighty, but also continuous and unbroken.

People sometimes say, “For a week or a month God kept me wonderfully. I lived in the light of His face, and I can’t tell you what joy I had in fellowship with Him. He blessed me in my work for others. He gave me souls, and at times I felt as if I were being carried up to heaven on eagles’ wings. But it didn’t continue. It was too good; it couldn’t last.” Some say, “I had to fall, to keep me humble.” Others say, “I know it was my own fault; but somehow you can’t always live up on the heights.”

Oh, beloved, why is this? Can there be any reason why God’s keeping should not be continuous and unbroken? Just think. All life is an unbroken continuity. If my life stopped for half an hour, I would be dead; my life would be gone. Life is continuous, and the life of God is the life of His Church, and the life of God is His almighty power working in us. God comes to us as the Almighty One and, without any conditions, offers to be my Keeper — and His keeping means that day by day and moment by moment God is going to keep us.

If I asked you, “Do you think God is able to keep you from actual sin for one day?” you would answer, “I don’t just know He is able; I think He has done it. There have been days when He kept my heart in His holy presence. Though I always had a sinful nature within me, He kept me from conscious, actual sin.”

Well, if He can do that for an hour or a day, why not for two days? Oh, let us make God’s omnipotence, as revealed in His Word, the measure of our expectations! Has God not said in His Word, “I, the Lord, do keep it, and will water it every moment” (Isa. 27:3)? What can that mean? Does “every moment” mean every moment? Did God promise of that vineyard of red wine that every moment He would water it, so that the heat of the sun and the scorching wind would never dry it up? Yes. In South Africa they sometimes make a graft and tie a bottle of water above it, so that every so often a drop falls to soak what they have wrapped around it. In this way the moisture is kept there without a break until the graft has had time to take, and can withstand the heat of the sun.

Will our God, in His tender love toward us, not keep us every moment when He has promised to? Oh, if only we once laid hold of this thought: our whole spiritual life is to be God’s doing — “It is God that worketh in us to will and to do of his good pleasure” (Phil. 2:13). Once we have faith to expect that from God, God will do everything for us.

The keeping is to be continuous. Every morning God will meet you as you wake. Don’t worry, “What if I forget to wake up in the morning thinking of Him — what will happen then?” If you trust your waking to God, God will meet you in the morning as you wake, with His divine sunshine and love. He will give you the awareness that all through the day you have God taking charge of you continuously with His almighty power. And God will meet you the next day and every day. Never mind if, as you practise this fellowship, failure sometimes comes. If you hold your position and say, “Lord, I am going to expect You to do Your utmost, and I am going to trust You day by day to keep me absolutely,” your faith will grow stronger and stronger, and you will know the keeping power of God without a break.

Kept Through Faith

And now the other side — believing. “Kept by the power of God through faith.” How should we think about this faith?

Faith Implies Helplessness

Let me say, first of all, that this faith means complete powerlessness and helplessness before God.

At the root of all faith there is a sense of helplessness. If I have some business to carry out — perhaps buying a house — the lawyer has to do the work of transferring the property into my name and making all the arrangements. I cannot do that work, and by trusting that agent I admit that I cannot do it. So faith always means helplessness. In many cases it means, “I could do it with a great deal of trouble, but someone else can do it better.” But in most cases it is utter helplessness: someone else must do it for me. And that is the secret of the spiritual life. A person must learn to say, “I give up everything. I have tried and longed and thought and prayed, but failure has come. God has blessed me and helped me, but still, in the long run, there has been so much sin and sadness.” What a change comes when a person is broken down like this into utter helplessness and despair of self, and says, “I can do nothing!”

Remember Paul. He was living a blessed life; he had been caught up into the third heaven. Then the thorn in the flesh came, “a messenger of Satan to buffet me.” And what happened? Paul could not understand it, and he prayed to the Lord three times to take it away. But the Lord said, in effect,

“No. You might exalt yourself, and so I have sent you this trial to keep you weak and humble.”

Then Paul learned a lesson he never forgot: to rejoice in his weaknesses. He said that the weaker he was, the better it was for him, because when he was weak, he was strong in his Lord Christ.

Do you want to enter what people call “the higher life”? Then go a step lower down. I remember Dr. Boardman telling how a gentleman once invited him to visit a factory where they made fine shot — I believe the workmen did it by pouring molten lead down from a great height. This gentleman wanted to take Dr. Boardman up to the top of the tower to see how the work was done. The doctor came to the tower, went in through the door and started up the stairs. But when he had gone a few steps, the gentleman called out,

“That’s the wrong way. You must come down this way; that staircase is locked.”

The gentleman took him a good many steps downstairs, and there a lift was ready to take him to the top. And Dr. Boardman said,

“I have learned a lesson: going down is often the best way to get up.”

Ah, yes — God will have to bring us very low. A sense of emptiness and despair and nothingness will have to come over us. It is when we sink down in utter helplessness that the everlasting God will reveal Himself in His power, and our hearts will learn to trust God alone.

What keeps us from trusting Him perfectly?

Many people say, “I believe what you say, but there is one difficulty. If my trust were perfect and always lasting, everything would come right, because I know God will honour trust. But how am I to get that trust?”

My answer is: “By the death of self. The great hindrance to trust is self-effort. As long as you hold on to your own wisdom and thoughts and strength, you cannot fully trust God. But when God breaks you down, when everything begins to grow dim before your eyes and you see that you understand nothing, then God is drawing near. If you will bow down in your nothingness and wait on God, He will become everything.”

As long as we are something, God cannot be everything, and His omnipotence cannot do its full work. That is the beginning of faith: utter despair of self, ceasing from man and from everything on earth, and finding our hope in God alone.

Faith Is Rest

And next, we must understand that faith is rest.

At the beginning of the life of faith, faith struggles; but as long as faith is struggling, it has not reached its full strength. When faith, in its struggling, comes to the end of itself and simply throws itself on God and rests on Him, then joy and victory come.

Perhaps I can make it clearer by telling the story of how the Keswick Convention began. Canon Battersby had been an evangelical clergyman of the Church of England for more than twenty years — a man of deep and tender godliness. But he had no sense of rest and victory over sin, and he was often deeply saddened by the thought of his stumbling and failure and sin. When he heard about the possibility of victory, he felt it was something to be desired, but it seemed he could not reach it. On one occasion he heard an address on “Rest and Faith,” taken from the story of the nobleman who came from Capernaum to Cana to ask Christ to heal his child. The address showed that the nobleman believed Christ could help him in a general way, but that he came to Jesus largely as an experiment. He hoped Christ would help him, but he had no assurance of that help. But what happened? When Christ said to him, “Go thy way, for thy child liveth,” the man believed the word Jesus spoke; he rested in that word. He had no proof that his child was well again, and he had a seven hours’ journey to walk back to Capernaum. He walked back, and on the way he met his servant and heard the first news that the child was well — that at one o’clock the previous afternoon, the very moment Jesus spoke to him, the fever had left the child. That father rested on the word of Jesus and His work. He went down to Capernaum and found his child well; he praised God, and he and his whole household became believers and disciples of Jesus.

Oh, friends, that is faith! When God comes to me with the promise of His keeping, and I have nothing on earth to trust in, I say to God, “Your word is enough: kept by the power of God.” That is faith; that is rest.

When Canon Battersby heard that address, he went home, and that night, in the darkness, he found rest. He rested on the word of Jesus. The next morning, in the streets of Oxford, he said to a friend, “I have found it!” Then he went and told others, and asked that the Keswick Convention be started, and that those at the convention with him should simply testify to what God had done.

It is a great thing when someone comes to rest on God’s almighty power for every moment of his life, in the face of coming temptations to temper and haste and anger and unlovingness and pride and sin. It is a great thing, facing all this, to enter into a covenant with the almighty Jehovah — not because of anything anyone says, or anything my heart feels, but on the strength of the Word of God: “Kept by the power of God through faith.”

Oh, let us tell God that we are going to put Him to the test to the very uttermost. Let us say, “We ask You for nothing more than You can give, but we want nothing less.” Let us say, “My God, let my life be a proof of what the almighty God can do.” Let these be the two attitudes of our souls every day: deep helplessness, and simple, childlike rest.

Faith Needs Fellowship

That brings me to just one more thought about faith: faith involves fellowship with God.

Many people want to take the Word and believe it, and they find they cannot. Ah, no! You cannot separate God from His Word. No goodness or power can be received apart from God Himself. If you want to enter this life of godliness, you must take time for fellowship with God.

People sometimes tell me, “My life is such a rush and bustle that I have no time for fellowship with God.” A dear missionary said to me, “People don’t know how we missionaries are tempted. I get up at five in the morning, and there are the local people waiting for their work orders. Then I have to go to the school and spend hours there. Then there is other work, and sixteen hours rush past, and I hardly get any time to be alone with God.”

Ah, there is the lack! I beg you, remember two things. I have not told you to trust the omnipotence of God as a thing, and I have not told you to trust the Word of God as a written book. I have told you to go to the God of omnipotence and the God of the Word. Deal with God as that nobleman dealt with the living Christ. Why was he able to believe the word Christ spoke to him? Because in the very eyes and tone and voice of Jesus, the Son of God, he saw and heard something that made him feel he could trust Him. And that is what Christ can do for you and me. Don’t try to stir up and rouse faith from within. How often I have tried that, and made a fool of myself! You cannot stir up faith from the depths of your own heart. Leave your heart alone, look into the face of Christ, and listen to what He tells you about how He will keep you. Look up into the face of your loving Father and spend time with Him every day. Begin a new life with the deep emptiness and poverty of someone who has nothing and wants to receive everything from Him, and with the deep restfulness of someone who rests on the living God, the almighty Jehovah. Then try God, and prove Him, if He will not open the windows of heaven and pour out a blessing that there shall not be room to receive it.

I close by asking: are you willing to experience to the very full the heavenly keeping for the heavenly inheritance? Robert Murray M’Cheyne says somewhere, “Oh, God, make me as holy as a pardoned sinner can be made.” If that prayer is in your heart, come now and let us enter afresh into a covenant with the everlasting and almighty Jehovah, and place ourselves in His hands — in great helplessness, but in great restfulness. And as we enter into our covenant, let us have this one prayer: that we may believe fully that the everlasting God is going to be our Companion, holding our hand every moment of the day; our Keeper, watching over us without a moment’s break; our Father, delighting always to reveal Himself in our souls. He has the power to let the sunshine of His love be with us all day long. Don’t be afraid that because you have your business you cannot have God with you always. Learn the lesson of the natural sun: it shines on you all day, and you enjoy its light; wherever you are, you have the sun, because God takes care that it shines on you. And God will take care that His own divine light shines on you, and that you remain in that light, if only you will trust Him for it. Let us trust God to do that, with a great and complete trust.

Here is the omnipotence of God, and here is faith reaching out to the full measure of that omnipotence. Shall we not say, “Everything that omnipotence can do, I am going to trust my God for”? Aren’t the two sides of this heavenly life wonderful? God’s omnipotence covers me, and my will, in all its littleness, rests in that omnipotence and rejoices in it!

Moment by moment, I’m kept in His love;

Moment by moment, I’ve life from above;

Looking to Jesus, the glory doth shine;

Moment by moment, Oh, Lord, I am Thine!
