If you hold your position and say, “Lord, I am going to expect You to do Your utmost, and I am going to trust You day by day to keep me absolutely,” your faith will grow stronger and stronger, and you will know the keeping power of God without a break. Kept Through Faith And now the other side — believing. “Kept by the power of God through faith.” How should we think about this faith? Faith Implies Helplessness Let me say, first of all, that this faith means complete powerlessness and helplessness before God. At the root of all faith there is a sense of helplessness. If I have some business to carry out — perhaps buying a house — the lawyer has to do the work of transferring the property into my name and making all the arrangements. I cannot do that work, and by trusting that agent I admit that I cannot do it. So faith always means helplessness. In many cases it means, “I could do it with a great deal of trouble, but someone else can do it better.” But in most cases it is utter helplessness: someone else must do it for me. And that is the secret of the spiritual life. A person must learn to say, “I give up everything. I have tried and longed and thought and prayed, but failure has come. God has blessed me and helped me, but still, in the long run, there has been so much sin and sadness.” What a change comes when a person is broken down like this into utter helplessness and despair of self, and says, “I can do nothing!” Remember Paul. He was living a blessed life; he had been caught up into the third heaven. Then the thorn in the flesh came, “a messenger of Satan to buffet me.” And what happened? Paul could not understand it, and he prayed to the Lord three times to take it away. But the Lord said, in effect, “No. You might exalt yourself, and so I have sent you this trial to keep you weak and humble.” Then Paul learned a lesson he never forgot: to rejoice in his weaknesses. He said that the weaker he was, the better it was for him, because when he was weak, he was strong in his Lord Christ. Do you want to enter what people call “the higher life”? Then go a step lower down. I remember Dr. Boardman telling how a gentleman once invited him to visit a factory where they made fine shot — I believe the workmen did it by pouring molten lead down from a great height. This gentleman wanted to take Dr. Boardman up to the top of the tower to see how the work was done. The doctor came to the tower, went in through the door and started up the stairs. But when he had gone a few steps, the gentleman called out, “That’s the wrong way. You must come down this way; that staircase is locked.” The gentleman took him a good many steps downstairs, and there a lift was ready to take him to the top. And Dr. Boardman said, “I have learned a lesson: going down is often the best way to get up.” Ah, yes — God will have to bring us very low. A sense of emptiness and despair and nothingness will have to come over us. It is when we sink down in utter helplessness that the everlasting God will reveal Himself in His power, and our hearts will learn to trust God alone. What keeps us from trusting Him perfectly? Many people say, “I believe what you say, but there is one difficulty. If my trust were perfect and always lasting, everything would come right, because I know God will honour trust. But how am I to get that trust?” My answer is: “By the death of self. The great hindrance to trust is self-effort. As long as you hold on to your own wisdom and thoughts and strength, you cannot fully trust God. But when God breaks you down, when everything begins to grow dim before your eyes and you see that you understand nothing, then God is drawing near. If you will bow down in your nothingness and wait on God, He will become everything.” As long as we are something, God cannot be everything, and His omnipotence cannot do its full work. That is the beginning of faith: utter despair of self, ceasing from man and from everything on earth, and finding our hope in God alone. Faith Is Rest And next, we must understand that faith is rest. At the beginning of the life of faith, faith struggles; but as long as faith is struggling, it has not reached its full strength. When faith, in its struggling, comes to the end of itself and simply throws itself on God and rests on Him, then joy and victory come. Perhaps I can make it clearer by telling the story of how the Keswick Convention began. Canon Battersby had been an evangelical clergyman of the Church of England for more than twenty years — a man of deep and tender godliness. But he had no sense of rest and victory over sin, and he was often deeply saddened by the thought of his stumbling and failure and sin. When he heard about the possibility of victory, he felt it was something to be desired, but it seemed he could not reach it. On one occasion he heard an address on “Rest and Faith,” taken from the story of the nobleman who came from Capernaum to Cana to ask Christ to heal his child. The address showed that the nobleman believed Christ could help him in a general way, but that he came to Jesus largely as an experiment. He hoped Christ would help him, but he had no assurance of that help. But what happened? When Christ said to him, “Go thy way, for thy child liveth,” the man believed the word Jesus spoke; he rested in that word. He had no proof that his child was well again, and he had a seven hours’ journey to walk back to Capernaum. He walked back, and on the way he met his servant and heard the first news that the child was well — that at one o’clock the previous afternoon, the very moment Jesus spoke to him, the fever had left the child. That father rested on the word of Jesus and His work. He went down to Capernaum and found his child well; he praised God, and he and his whole household became believers and disciples of Jesus. Oh, friends, that is faith! When God comes to me with the promise of His keeping, and I have nothing on earth to trust in, I say to God, “Your word is enough: kept by the power of God.” That is faith; that is rest. When Canon Battersby heard that address, he went home, and that night, in the darkness, he found rest. He rested on the word of Jesus. The next morning, in the streets of Oxford, he said to a friend, “I have found it!” Then he went and told others, and asked that the Keswick Convention be started, and that those at the convention with him should simply testify to what God had done. It is a great thing when someone comes to rest on God’s almighty power for every moment of his life, in the face of coming temptations to temper and haste and anger and unlovingness and pride and sin. It is a great thing, facing all this, to enter into a covenant with the almighty Jehovah — not because of anything anyone says, or anything my heart feels, but on the strength of the Word of God: “Kept by the power of God through faith.” Oh, let us tell God that we are going to put Him to the test to the very uttermost. Let us say, “We ask You for nothing more than You can give, but we want nothing less.” Let us say, “My God, let my life be a proof of what the almighty God can do.” Let these be the two attitudes of our souls every day: deep helplessness, and simple, childlike rest. Faith Needs Fellowship That brings me to just one more thought about faith: faith involves fellowship with God. Many people want to take the Word and believe it, and they find they cannot. Ah, no! You cannot separate God from His Word. No goodness or power can be received apart from God Himself. If you want to enter this life of godliness, you must take time for fellowship with God. People sometimes tell me, “My life is such a rush and bustle that I have no time for fellowship with God.” A dear missionary said to me, “People don’t know how we missionaries are tempted. I get up at five in the morning, and there are the local people waiting for their work orders. Then I have to go to the school and spend hours there. Then there is other work, and sixteen hours rush past, and I hardly get any time to be alone with God.” Ah, there is the lack! I beg you, remember two things. I have not told you to trust the omnipotence of God as a thing, and I have not told you to trust the Word of God as a written book. I have told you to go to the God of omnipotence and the God of the Word. Deal with God as that nobleman dealt with the living Christ. Why was he able to believe the word Christ spoke to him? Because in the very eyes and tone and voice of Jesus, the Son of God, he saw and heard something that made him feel he could trust Him. And that is what Christ can do for you and me. Don’t try to stir up and rouse faith from within. How often I have tried that, and made a fool of myself! You cannot stir up faith from the depths of your own heart. Leave your heart alone, look into the face of Christ, and listen to what He tells you about how He will keep you. Look up into the face of your loving Father and spend time with Him every day. Begin a new life with the deep emptiness and poverty of someone who has nothing and wants to receive everything from Him, and with the deep restfulness of someone who rests on the living God, the almighty Jehovah. Then try God, and prove Him, if He will not open the windows of heaven and pour out a blessing that there shall not be room to receive it. I close by asking: are you willing to experience to the very full the heavenly keeping for the heavenly inheritance? Robert Murray M’Cheyne says somewhere, “Oh, God, make me as holy as a pardoned sinner can be made.” If that prayer is in your heart, come now and let us enter afresh into a covenant with the everlasting and almighty Jehovah, and place ourselves in His hands — in great helplessness, but in great restfulness. And as we enter into our covenant, let us have this one prayer: that we may believe fully that the everlasting God is going to be our Companion, holding our hand every moment of the day; our Keeper, watching over us without a moment’s break; our Father, delighting always to reveal Himself in our souls. He has the power to let the sunshine of His love be with us all day long. Don’t be afraid that because you have your business you cannot have God with you always. Learn the lesson of the natural sun: it shines on you all day, and you enjoy its light; wherever you are, you have the sun, because God takes care that it shines on you. And God will take care that His own divine light shines on you, and that you remain in that light, if only you will trust Him for it. Let us trust God to do that, with a great and complete trust. Here is the omnipotence of God, and here is faith reaching out to the full measure of that omnipotence. Shall we not say, “Everything that omnipotence can do, I am going to trust my God for”? Aren’t the two sides of this heavenly life wonderful? God’s omnipotence covers me, and my will, in all its littleness, rests in that omnipotence and rejoices in it! Moment by moment, I’m kept in His love; Moment by moment, I’ve life from above; Looking to Jesus, the glory doth shine; Moment by moment, Oh, Lord, I am Thine!

fields.title: Ye are the Branches
fields.body_html:
An Address to Christian Workers

Everything depends on our being right ourselves, in Christ. If I want good apples, I must have a good apple tree; and if I look after the health of the apple tree, it will give me good apples. It is exactly the same with our Christian life and work. If our life with Christ is right, everything will come right. There may be a need for instruction and suggestions and help and training in the various areas of the work, and all of that has value. But in the long run, the greatest essential is to have the full life in Christ — in other words, to have Christ in us, working through us. I know how much there often is to unsettle us or to raise anxious questions. But the Master has such a blessing for every one of us — such perfect peace and rest, such joy and strength — if only we can come into the right attitude toward Him and be kept in it.

I will take my text from the parable of the Vine and the Branches, in John 15:5: “I am the vine, ye are the branches.” Especially these words: “Ye are the branches.”

What a simple thing it is to be a branch — the branch of a tree or the branch of a vine! The branch grows out of the vine or the tree, and there it lives and grows, and in due time bears fruit. It has no responsibility except simply to receive sap and nourishment from the root and the stem. If only we knew, by the Holy Spirit, our relationship to Jesus Christ, our work would be turned into the brightest and most heavenly thing on earth. Instead of weariness of soul or exhaustion, our work would be like a new experience, joining us to Jesus as nothing else can. For sadly, isn’t it often true that our work comes between us and Jesus? What folly! The very work that He has to do in me, and that I do for Him, I take up in such a way that it separates me from Christ. Many a labourer in the vineyard has complained that he has too much work and no time for close communion with Jesus; that his everyday work weakens his desire to pray; and that dealing so much with people darkens his spiritual life. What a sad thought — that bearing fruit should separate the branch from the vine! That can only be because we have thought of our work as something other than the branch bearing fruit. May God deliver us from every false idea about the Christian life.

Now, just a few thoughts about this blessed branch-life.

Absolute Dependence

In the first place, it is a life of absolute dependence. The branch has nothing of its own; it depends on the vine for everything. Absolute dependence is one of the most solemn and precious of thoughts. Some years ago a great German theologian wrote two large volumes to show that the whole of Calvin’s theology is summed up in that one principle of absolute dependence on God — and he was right. Another great writer has said that absolute, unchangeable dependence on God alone is the essence of the religion of angels, and should be the essence of ours too. God is everything to the angels, and He is willing to be everything to the Christian. If I can learn to depend on God every moment of the day, everything will come right. You will find the higher life if you depend absolutely on God.

And here we find it in the vine and the branches. Let every vine you see, every bunch of grapes that comes to your table, remind you that the branch is absolutely dependent on the vine. The vine has to do the work, and the branch enjoys the fruit of it.

What does the vine have to do? It has a great work to do. It has to send its roots out into the soil and search underground for nourishment — the roots often spread a long way out — and drink in the moisture. Put certain kinds of manure in certain places, and the vine will send its roots there. Then, in its roots or stems, it turns the moisture and manure into the particular sap that will produce the fruit. The vine does the work; the branch simply has to receive from the vine the sap that is turned into grapes. I have been told that at Hampton Court, near London, there is a vine that at times bore a couple of thousand bunches of grapes, and people were astonished at its great growth and rich crop. Later the reason was discovered. The River Thames runs not far away, and the vine had stretched its roots hundreds of yards underground until it reached the riverbank. There, in all the rich mud of the riverbed, it had found abundant nourishment and moisture, and the roots had drawn the sap all that distance up into the vine — and the result was that abundant, rich harvest. The vine had the work to do, and the branches simply had to depend on the vine and receive what it gave.

Is that literally true of my Lord Jesus? Am I to understand that when I have work to do — when I have to preach a sermon, or speak to a Bible class, or go out and visit the poor and neglected — all the responsibility for the work rests on Christ?

That is exactly what Christ wants you to understand. Christ wants the very foundation of all your work to be the simple, blessed awareness: Christ must take care of everything.

And how does He fulfil the trust we place in Him by that dependence? He does it by sending down the Holy Spirit — not just now and then as a special gift. Remember, the relationship between the vine and the branches is such that the living connection is kept up hourly, daily, unceasingly. The sap does not flow for a while, then stop, then flow again; it flows from the vine to the branches from moment to moment. In just the same way, my Lord Jesus wants me to take that blessed position as a worker. Morning by morning, day by day, hour by hour, step by step, in every piece of work I go out to do, He wants me simply to remain before Him in the utter helplessness of one who knows nothing, is nothing and can do nothing. Oh, beloved workers, study that word nothing. You sometimes sing, “Oh, to be nothing, nothing”; but have you really studied that word, and prayed every day and worshipped God in its light? Do you know the blessedness of that word nothing?

If I am something, then God is not everything. But when I become nothing, God can become everything, and the everlasting God in Christ can reveal Himself fully. That is the higher life. We need to become nothing. Someone has rightly said that the seraphim and cherubim are flames of fire because they know they are nothing, and so they let God fill them with His fullness and His glory and brightness. Oh, become nothing in deep reality! And as a worker, study only one thing: to become poorer and lower and more helpless, so that Christ may do everything in you.

Workers, here is your first lesson: learn to be nothing; learn to be helpless. The person who has something is not absolutely dependent; the person who has nothing is absolutely dependent. Absolute dependence on God is the secret of all power in work. The branch has nothing except what it receives from the vine, and you and I can have nothing except what we receive from Jesus.

Deep Restfulness

Second, the life of the branch is not only a life of complete dependence but of deep restfulness.

Suppose that little branch could think and feel and speak — that branch on the Hampton Court vine, or on one of the million vines we have in our sunny land of South Africa. Suppose we had a little branch here today to talk to us, and we said to it, “Come, branch of the vine, I want to learn from you how I can be a true branch of the living Vine.” What would it answer? The little branch would whisper:

“Man, I hear that you are wise, and I know you can do a great many wonderful things. I know you have been given much strength and wisdom, but I have one lesson for you. With all your hurry and effort in Christ’s work, you never prosper. The first thing you need is to come and rest in your Lord Jesus. That is what I do. Years and years have passed since I grew out of that vine, and all I have done is simply rest in the vine. When spring came, I had no anxious thought or care. The vine began to pour its sap into me and to give me bud and leaf. When summer came, I had no care; in the great heat I trusted the vine to bring moisture to keep me fresh. And at harvest time, when the owner came to pick the grapes, I had no care. If there was anything wrong with the grapes, the owner never blamed the branch; the blame always fell on the vine. So if you want to be a true branch of Christ, the living Vine, just rest on Him. Let Christ carry the responsibility.”

You say, “Won’t that make me lazy?”

I tell you it will not. No one who learns to rest on the living Christ can become lazy, because the closer your contact with Christ, the more the Spirit of His zeal and love will be pressed into you. But oh, begin to work in the midst of your complete dependence by adding to it this deep restfulness. Sometimes a person tries and tries to be dependent on Christ, but he worries himself about this absolute dependence; he tries and cannot get it. Let him instead sink down into complete restfulness every day.

In Thy strong hand I lay me down.

So shall the work be done;

For who can work so wondrously

As the Almighty One?

Worker, take your place every day at the feet of Jesus, in the blessed peace and rest that come from knowing —

I have no care, my cares are His!

I have no fear, He cares for all my fears.

Come, children of God, and understand that it is the Lord Jesus who wants to work through you. You complain of a lack of fervent love. It will come from Jesus. He will put into your heart the divine love with which you can love people. That is the meaning of the assurance, “The love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Spirit” (Rom. 5:5), and of that other word, “The love of Christ constraineth us” (2 Cor. 5:14). Christ can give you a fountain of love, so that you cannot help loving the most wretched and the most ungrateful, or those who have worn you out until now. Rest in Christ, who can give wisdom and strength, and you have no idea how often that restfulness will turn out to be the very best part of your message. You plead with people and you argue with them, and they get the idea, “Here is a man arguing and struggling with me.” All they feel is, “Here are two men dealing with each other.” But if you will let the deep rest of God come over you — the rest in Christ Jesus, the peace and rest and holiness of heaven — that restfulness will bring a blessing to their hearts even more than the words you speak.

Much Fruitfulness

Third, the branch teaches a lesson of much fruitfulness.

The Lord Jesus Christ repeated that word fruit often in that parable. He spoke first of fruit, then of more fruit, then of much fruit. Yes, you are appointed not only to bear fruit but to bear much fruit. “Herein is my Father glorified, that ye bear much fruit” (John 15:8). First of all, Christ said, “I am the Vine, and my Father is the Husbandman” — the Husbandman who has charge of both Him and you. It is God who will watch over the connection between Christ and the branches, and it is in the power of God, through Christ, that we are to bear fruit.

Oh, Christians, you know this world is perishing for lack of workers. And it is not only more workers it lacks. The workers themselves are saying, some more earnestly than others, “We need not only more workers; we need our workers to have a new power, a different life, so that we workers can bring more blessing.” Children of God, I appeal to you. You know what trouble you will take in a case of sickness, say. You have a dear friend who seems to be in danger of death, and nothing can refresh that friend as much as a few grapes — and they are out of season. Yet what trouble you will take to get the grapes that are to nourish your dying friend! And oh, all around you there are people who never go to church, and so many who go to church but do not know Christ. Yet the heavenly grapes, the grapes of the heavenly Vine, cannot be had at any price, except as the child of God bears them out of his inner life in fellowship with Christ. Unless the children of God are filled with the sap of the heavenly Vine — unless they are filled with the Holy Spirit and the love of Jesus — they cannot bear much of the real heavenly grape. We all admit that there is a great deal of work — a great deal of preaching and teaching and visiting, a great deal of machinery, a great deal of earnest effort of every kind — but not much evidence of the power of God in it.

What is lacking? What is lacking is a close connection between the worker and the heavenly Vine. Christ, the heavenly Vine, has blessings He could pour out on tens of thousands who are perishing. Christ, the heavenly Vine, has power to provide the heavenly grapes. But “Ye are the branches,” and you cannot bear heavenly fruit unless you are closely connected with Jesus Christ.

Don’t confuse work with fruit. There may be a great deal of work for Christ that is not the fruit of the heavenly Vine. Don’t seek work only. Oh, study this question of fruit-bearing! It means the very life, the very power, the very spirit and the very love within the heart of the Son of God — it means the heavenly Vine Himself coming into your heart and mine.

You know there are different kinds of grapes, each with a different name, and every vine produces exactly the particular aroma and juice that give its grape its own flavour and taste. In the same way, there is in the heart of Christ Jesus a life and a love, a Spirit and a blessing and a power for people, that are entirely heavenly and divine, and that will come down into our hearts. Keep in close connection with the heavenly Vine, and say:

“Lord Jesus, nothing less than the sap that flows through You, nothing less than the Spirit of Your divine life, is what we ask. Lord Jesus, I pray, let Your Spirit flow through me in all my work for You.”

I tell you again: the sap of the heavenly Vine is nothing other than the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit is the life of the heavenly Vine, and what you must receive from Christ is nothing less than a strong inflow of the Holy Spirit. You need it enormously, and you need nothing more than that. Remember it. Don’t expect Christ to give a bit of strength here, a bit of blessing there, and a bit of help somewhere else. Just as the vine does its work by giving its own particular sap to the branch, so expect Christ to give His own Holy Spirit into your heart, and then you will bear much fruit. And if you have only begun to bear fruit, and you are listening to Christ’s words in the parable — “more fruit,” “much fruit” — remember that to bear more fruit you simply need more of Jesus in your life and heart.

We ministers of the gospel — how easily we fall into a condition of work, work, work! We pray over it, but the freshness and buoyancy and joy of the heavenly life are not always there. Let us seek to understand that the life of the branch is a life of much fruit, because it is a life rooted in Christ, the living, heavenly Vine.

Close Communion

Fourth, the life of the branch is a life of close communion.

Let us ask again: what does the branch have to do? You know that precious, inexhaustible word Christ used: Abide. Your life is to be an abiding life. And what is the abiding to be like? It is to be just like the branch in the vine, abiding every minute of the day. There are the branches, in close communion, unbroken communion, with the vine from January to December. And can I not live every day — it seems to me almost terrible that we should even ask the question — can I not live in abiding communion with the heavenly Vine?

You say, “But I am so busy with other things.”

You may have ten hours of hard work every day, during which your mind has to be busy with earthly things; God arranges it that way. But abiding is the work of the heart, not of the brain. It is the work of the heart clinging to Jesus and resting in Him, a work in which the Holy Spirit joins us to Christ Jesus. Oh, do believe that deeper down than the brain, deep in the inner life, you can abide in Christ, so that every moment you are free, the awareness will come:

“Blessed Jesus, I am still in You.”

If you will learn to set other work aside for a time and get into this abiding contact with the heavenly Vine, you will find that fruit will come.

How does this abiding communion apply to our lives? What does it mean?

It means close fellowship with Christ in secret prayer. I am sure there are Christians who really long for the higher life. Sometimes they have received a great blessing, and at times they have known a great inflow of heavenly joy and a great outflow of heavenly gladness — and yet after a while it has passed away. They have not understood that close, personal, real communion with Christ is an absolute necessity for daily life. Take time to be alone with Christ. Nothing in heaven or on earth can free you from the need for that, if you are to be happy and holy Christians.

Oh, how many Christians look on being often alone with God as a burden and a tax, a duty and a difficulty! That is the great hindrance to our Christian life everywhere. We need more quiet fellowship with God. And I tell you in the name of the heavenly Vine that you cannot be healthy branches — branches into which the heavenly sap can flow — unless you take plenty of time for communion with God. If you are not willing to sacrifice time to be alone with Him, and to give Him time every day to work in you and to keep up the connection between you and Himself, He cannot give you the blessing of His unbroken fellowship. Jesus Christ asks you to live in close communion with Him. Let every heart say, “O Christ, this is what I long for; this is what I choose.” And He will gladly give it to you.

Absolute Surrender

And finally, the life of the branch is a life of absolute surrender.

This word, absolute surrender, is a great and solemn word, and I believe we do not understand what it means. Yet the little branch preaches it.

“Do you have anything to do, little branch, besides bearing grapes?”

“No, nothing.”

“Are you fit for nothing else?”

Fit for nothing! The Bible says that a piece of vine cannot even be used to make a peg; it is fit for nothing but to be burned.

“And now, little branch, what do you understand about your relationship to the vine?”

“My relationship is simply this: I am utterly given up to the vine, and the vine can give me as much or as little sap as it chooses. Here I am at its disposal, and the vine can do with me whatever it likes.”

Oh, friends, we need this absolute surrender to the Lord Jesus Christ. The more I speak, the more I feel that this is one of the hardest points to make clear, and one of the most important and necessary to explain — what this absolute surrender is. It is often easy for a person, or a group of people, to come forward and offer themselves to God for entire consecration and say, “Lord, it is my desire to give myself up entirely to You.” That is very valuable, and it often brings very rich blessing. But the one question I ought to study quietly is: what does absolute surrender mean?

It means that, just as literally as Christ was given up entirely to God, I am given up entirely to Christ. Is that too strong? Some think so. Some think it can never be: that just as entirely and absolutely as Christ gave up His life to do nothing but seek the Father’s pleasure and to depend on the Father absolutely and completely, so I am to do nothing but seek the pleasure of Christ. But it really is true. Christ Jesus came to breathe His own Spirit into us, to make us find our very highest happiness in living entirely for God, just as He did. Oh, beloved brothers and sisters, if that is so, then I ought to say:

“Yes — as true as it is of that little branch of the vine, so true, by God’s grace, I want it to be of me. I want to live day by day in such a way that Christ can do with me whatever He wills.”

Ah, here is the terrible mistake that lies at the root of so much of our religion. A person thinks:

“I have my business and my family duties and my responsibilities as a citizen, and I can’t change any of that. And now, alongside all of it, I am to fit in religion and the service of God, as something that will keep me from sin. God help me to do my duties properly!”

This is not right. When Christ came, He came and bought the sinner with His blood. If there were a slave market here and I bought a slave, I would take that slave away from his old surroundings to my own house. He would live in my house as my personal property, and I could give him orders all day long. And if he were a faithful slave, he would live as one with no will and no interests of his own; his one concern would be to promote his master’s welfare and honour. In the same way I, who have been bought with the blood of Christ, have been bought to live every day with one thought: how can I please my Master?

Oh, we find the Christian life so difficult because we look for God’s blessing while we go on living in our own will. We would be glad to live the Christian life to suit ourselves. We make our own plans and choose our own work, and then we ask the Lord Jesus to come in and make sure that sin does not get too much of a hold on us and that we do not go too far wrong; we ask Him to come in and give us a certain amount of His blessing. But our relationship to Jesus ought to be such that we are entirely at His disposal, and every day we come to Him humbly and plainly and say:

“Lord, is there anything in me that is not in line with Your will, that has not been ordered by You, or that is not entirely given up to You?”

Oh, if we would wait, and wait patiently, I tell you what the result would be. A relationship between us and Christ would spring up so close and so tender that afterwards we would be amazed at how we could ever have lived with the idea, “I am surrendered to Christ.” We would feel how distant our fellowship with Him had been before, and we would find that He can — and really does — come and take actual possession of us, and give unbroken fellowship all day long. The branch calls us to absolute surrender.

I am not speaking now so much about giving up sins. There are people who need that — people with violent tempers, bad habits and actual sins they commit from time to time, which they have never given up into the very bosom of the Lamb of God. I beg you, if you are branches of the living Vine, don’t hold back a single sin. I know there are a great many difficulties about this question of holiness. I know that not everyone thinks exactly the same about it. That would matter relatively little to me if I could see that everyone was honestly longing to be free from every sin. But I am afraid that, without realising it, many hearts make compromises with the idea that we cannot be without sin — that we must sin a little every day, that we cannot help it. Oh, if only people would really cry to God, “Lord, do keep me from sin!” Give yourself utterly to Jesus, and ask Him to do His very utmost for you in keeping you from sin.

There is a great deal in our work, in our church and in our surroundings that we found already in the world when we were born into it. It has grown up all around us, and we think it is all right and cannot be changed. We don’t come to the Lord Jesus and ask Him about it. Oh, Christians, I urge you: bring everything into relationship with Jesus and say:

“Lord, everything in my life must be in the most complete harmony with my position as a branch of You, the blessed Vine.”

Let your surrender to Christ be absolute. I don’t fully understand that word surrender; every so often it takes on new meanings, and from time to time it grows immensely larger. But I urge you to say it out loud: “Absolute surrender to You, O Christ, is what I have chosen.” And Christ will show you what is not according to His mind, and lead you on to deeper and higher blessedness.

In conclusion, let me gather it all up in one sentence. Christ Jesus said, “I am the Vine, ye are the branches.” In other words: “I, the living One, who have given myself so completely to you, am the Vine. You cannot trust me too much. I am the almighty Worker, full of divine life and power.” You are the branches of the Lord Jesus Christ. If you are aware in your heart that you are not a strong, healthy, fruit-bearing branch — not closely joined to Jesus, not living in Him as you should — then listen to Him saying: “I am the Vine. I will receive you, I will draw you to myself, I will bless you, I will strengthen you, I will fill you with my Spirit. I, the Vine, have taken you to be my branches; I have given myself utterly to you. Children, give yourselves utterly to me. As God, I have surrendered myself absolutely to you; I became man and died for you so that I might be entirely yours. Come and surrender yourselves entirely to be mine.”

What will our answer be? Oh, let it be a prayer from the depths of our hearts that the living Christ may take each one of us and join us closely to Himself. Let our prayer be that He, the living Vine, will so join each of us to Himself that we go away with our hearts singing, “He is my Vine, and I am His branch — I want nothing more — now I have the everlasting Vine.” Then, when you are alone with Him, worship and adore Him, praise Him and trust Him, love Him and wait for His love. “You are my Vine, and I am Your branch. It is enough; my soul is satisfied.”

Glory to His blessed name!
fields.body_text: An Address to Christian Workers Everything depends on our being right ourselves, in Christ. If I want good apples, I must have a good apple tree; and if I look after the health of the apple tree, it will give me good apples. It is exactly the same with our Christian life and work. If our life with Christ is right, everything will come right. There may be a need for instruction and suggestions and help and training in the various areas of the work, and all of that has value. But in the long run, the greatest essential is to have the full life in Christ — in other words, to have Christ in us, working through us. I know how much there often is to unsettle us or to raise anxious questions. But the Master has such a blessing for every one of us — such perfect peace and rest, such joy and strength — if only we can come into the right attitude toward Him and be kept in it. I will take my text from the parable of the Vine and the Branches, in John 15:5: “I am the vine, ye are the branches.” Especially these words: “Ye are the branches.” What a simple thing it is to be a branch — the branch of a tree or the branch of a vine! The branch grows out of the vine or the tree, and there it lives and grows, and in due time bears fruit. It has no responsibility except simply to receive sap and nourishment from the root and the stem. If only we knew, by the Holy Spirit, our relationship to Jesus Christ, our work would be turned into the brightest and most heavenly thing on earth. Instead of weariness of soul or exhaustion, our work would be like a new experience, joining us to Jesus as nothing else can. For sadly, isn’t it often true that our work comes between us and Jesus? What folly! The very work that He has to do in me, and that I do for Him, I take up in such a way that it separates me from Christ. Many a labourer in the vineyard has complained that he has too much work and no time for close communion with Jesus; that his everyday work weakens his desire to pray; and that dealing so much with people darkens his spiritual life. What a sad thought — that bearing fruit should separate the branch from the vine! That can only be because we have thought of our work as something other than the branch bearing fruit. May God deliver us from every false idea about the Christian life. Now, just a few thoughts about this blessed branch-life. Absolute Dependence In the first place, it is a life of absolute dependence. The branch has nothing of its own; it depends on the vine for everything. Absolute dependence is one of the most solemn and precious of thoughts. Some years ago a great German theologian wrote two large volumes to show that the whole of Calvin’s theology is summed up in that one principle of absolute dependence on God — and he was right. Another great writer has said that absolute, unchangeable dependence on God alone is the essence of the religion of angels, and should be the essence of ours too. God is everything to the angels, and He is willing to be everything to the Christian. If I can learn to depend on God every moment of the day, everything will come right. You will find the higher life if you depend absolutely on God. And here we find it in the vine and the branches. Let every vine you see, every bunch of grapes that comes to your table, remind you that the branch is absolutely dependent on the vine. The vine has to do the work, and the branch enjoys the fruit of it. What does the vine have to do? It has a great work to do. It has to send its roots out into the soil and search underground for nourishment — the roots often spread a long way out — and drink in the moisture. Put certain kinds of manure in certain places, and the vine will send its roots there. Then, in its roots or stems, it turns the moisture and manure into the particular sap that will produce the fruit. The vine does the work; the branch simply has to receive from the vine the sap that is turned into grapes. I have been told that at Hampton Court, near London, there is a vine that at times bore a couple of thousand bunches of grapes, and people were astonished at its great growth and rich crop. Later the reason was discovered. The River Thames runs not far away, and the vine had stretched its roots hundreds of yards underground until it reached the riverbank. There, in all the rich mud of the riverbed, it had found abundant nourishment and moisture, and the roots had drawn the sap all that distance up into the vine — and the result was that abundant, rich harvest. The vine had the work to do, and the branches simply had to depend on the vine and receive what it gave. Is that literally true of my Lord Jesus? Am I to understand that when I have work to do — when I have to preach a sermon, or speak to a Bible class, or go out and visit the poor and neglected — all the responsibility for the work rests on Christ? That is exactly what Christ wants you to understand. Christ wants the very foundation of all your work to be the simple, blessed awareness: Christ must take care of everything. And how does He fulfil the trust we place in Him by that dependence? He does it by sending down the Holy Spirit — not just now and then as a special gift. Remember, the relationship between the vine and the branches is such that the living connection is kept up hourly, daily, unceasingly. The sap does not flow for a while, then stop, then flow again; it flows from the vine to the branches from moment to moment. In just the same way, my Lord Jesus wants me to take that blessed position as a worker. Morning by morning, day by day, hour by hour, step by step, in every piece of work I go out to do, He wants me simply to remain before Him in the utter helplessness of one who knows nothing, is nothing and can do nothing. Oh, beloved workers, study that word nothing. You sometimes sing, “Oh, to be nothing, nothing”; but have you really studied that word, and prayed every day and worshipped God in its light? Do you know the blessedness of that word nothing? If I am something, then God is not everything. But when I become nothing, God can become everything, and the everlasting God in Christ can reveal Himself fully. That is the higher life. We need to become nothing. Someone has rightly said that the seraphim and cherubim are flames of fire because they know they are nothing, and so they let God fill them with His fullness and His glory and brightness. Oh, become nothing in deep reality! And as a worker, study only one thing: to become poorer and lower and more helpless, so that Christ may do everything in you. Workers, here is your first lesson: learn to be nothing; learn to be helpless. The person who has something is not absolutely dependent; the person who has nothing is absolutely dependent. Absolute dependence on God is the secret of all power in work. The branch has nothing except what it receives from the vine, and you and I can have nothing except what we receive from Jesus. Deep Restfulness Second, the life of the branch is not only a life of complete dependence but of deep restfulness. Suppose that little branch could think and feel and speak — that branch on the Hampton Court vine, or on one of the million vines we have in our sunny land of South Africa. Suppose we had a little branch here today to talk to us, and we said to it, “Come, branch of the vine, I want to learn from you how I can be a true branch of the living Vine.” What would it answer? The little branch would whisper: “Man, I hear that you are wise, and I know you can do a great many wonderful things. I know you have been given much strength and wisdom, but I have one lesson for you. With all your hurry and effort in Christ’s work, you never prosper. The first thing you need is to come and rest in your Lord Jesus. That is what I do. Years and years have passed since I grew out of that vine, and all I have done is simply rest in the vine. When spring came, I had no anxious thought or care. The vine began to pour its sap into me and to give me bud and leaf. When summer came, I had no care; in the great heat I trusted the vine to bring moisture to keep me fresh. And at harvest time, when the owner came to pick the grapes, I had no care. If there was anything wrong with the grapes, the owner never blamed the branch; the blame always fell on the vine. So if you want to be a true branch of Christ, the living Vine, just rest on Him. Let Christ carry the responsibility.” You say, “Won’t that make me lazy?” I tell you it will not. No one who learns to rest on the living Christ can become lazy, because the closer your contact with Christ, the more the Spirit of His zeal and love will be pressed into you. But oh, begin to work in the midst of your complete dependence by adding to it this deep restfulness. Sometimes a person tries and tries to be dependent on Christ, but he worries himself about this absolute dependence; he tries and cannot get it. Let him instead sink down into complete restfulness every day. In Thy strong hand I lay me down. So shall the work be done; For who can work so wondrously As the Almighty One? Worker, take your place every day at the feet of Jesus, in the blessed peace and rest that come from knowing — I have no care, my cares are His! I have no fear, He cares for all my fears. Come, children of God, and understand that it is the Lord Jesus who wants to work through you. You complain of a lack of fervent love. It will come from Jesus. He will put into your heart the divine love with which you can love people. That is the meaning of the assurance, “The love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Spirit” (Rom. 5:5), and of that other word, “The love of Christ constraineth us” (2 Cor. 5:14). Christ can give you a fountain of love, so that you cannot help loving the most wretched and the most ungrateful, or those who have worn you out until now. Rest in Christ, who can give wisdom and strength, and you have no idea how often that restfulness will turn out to be the very best part of your message. You plead with people and you argue with them, and they get the idea, “Here is a man arguing and struggling with me.” All they feel is, “Here are two men dealing with each other.” But if you will let the deep rest of God come over you — the rest in Christ Jesus, the peace and rest and holiness of heaven — that restfulness will bring a blessing to their hearts even more than the words you speak. Much Fruitfulness Third, the branch teaches a lesson of much fruitfulness. The Lord Jesus Christ repeated that word fruit often in that parable. He spoke first of fruit, then of more fruit, then of much fruit. Yes, you are appointed not only to bear fruit but to bear much fruit. “Herein is my Father glorified, that ye bear much fruit” (John 15:8). First of all, Christ said, “I am the Vine, and my Father is the Husbandman” — the Husbandman who has charge of both Him and you. It is God who will watch over the connection between Christ and the branches, and it is in the power of God, through Christ, that we are to bear fruit. Oh, Christians, you know this world is perishing for lack of workers. And it is not only more workers it lacks. The workers themselves are saying, some more earnestly than others, “We need not only more workers; we need our workers to have a new power, a different life, so that we workers can bring more blessing.” Children of God, I appeal to you. You know what trouble you will take in a case of sickness, say. You have a dear friend who seems to be in danger of death, and nothing can refresh that friend as much as a few grapes — and they are out of season. Yet what trouble you will take to get the grapes that are to nourish your dying friend! And oh, all around you there are people who never go to church, and so many who go to church but do not know Christ. Yet the heavenly grapes, the grapes of the heavenly Vine, cannot be had at any price, except as the child of God bears them out of his inner life in fellowship with Christ. Unless the children of God are filled with the sap of the heavenly Vine — unless they are filled with the Holy Spirit and the love of Jesus — they cannot bear much of the real heavenly grape. We all admit that there is a great deal of work — a great deal of preaching and teaching and visiting, a great deal of machinery, a great deal of earnest effort of every kind — but not much evidence of the power of God in it. What is lacking? What is lacking is a close connection between the worker and the heavenly Vine. Christ, the heavenly Vine, has blessings He could pour out on tens of thousands who are perishing. Christ, the heavenly Vine, has power to provide the heavenly grapes. But “Ye are the branches,” and you cannot bear heavenly fruit unless you are closely connected with Jesus Christ. Don’t confuse work with fruit. There may be a great deal of work for Christ that is not the fruit of the heavenly Vine. Don’t seek work only. Oh, study this question of fruit-bearing! It means the very life, the very power, the very spirit and the very love within the heart of the Son of God — it means the heavenly Vine Himself coming into your heart and mine. You know there are different kinds of grapes, each with a different name, and every vine produces exactly the particular aroma and juice that give its grape its own flavour and taste. In the same way, there is in the heart of Christ Jesus a life and a love, a Spirit and a blessing and a power for people, that are entirely heavenly and divine, and that will come down into our hearts. Keep in close connection with the heavenly Vine, and say: “Lord Jesus, nothing less than the sap that flows through You, nothing less than the Spirit of Your divine life, is what we ask. Lord Jesus, I pray, let Your Spirit flow through me in all my work for You.” I tell you again: the sap of the heavenly Vine is nothing other than the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit is the life of the heavenly Vine, and what you must receive from Christ is nothing less than a strong inflow of the Holy Spirit. You need it enormously, and you need nothing more than that. Remember it. Don’t expect Christ to give a bit of strength here, a bit of blessing there, and a bit of help somewhere else. Just as the vine does its work by giving its own particular sap to the branch, so expect Christ to give His own Holy Spirit into your heart, and then you will bear much fruit. And if you have only begun to bear fruit, and you are listening to Christ’s words in the parable — “more fruit,” “much fruit” — remember that to bear more fruit you simply need more of Jesus in your life and heart. We ministers of the gospel — how easily we fall into a condition of work, work, work! We pray over it, but the freshness and buoyancy and joy of the heavenly life are not always there. Let us seek to understand that the life of the branch is a life of much fruit, because it is a life rooted in Christ, the living, heavenly Vine. Close Communion Fourth, the life of the branch is a life of close communion. Let us ask again: what does the branch have to do? You know that precious, inexhaustible word Christ used: Abide. Your life is to be an abiding life. And what is the abiding to be like? It is to be just like the branch in the vine, abiding every minute of the day. There are the branches, in close communion, unbroken communion, with the vine from January to December. And can I not live every day — it seems to me almost terrible that we should even ask the question — can I not live in abiding communion with the heavenly Vine? You say, “But I am so busy with other things.” You may have ten hours of hard work every day, during which your mind has to be busy with earthly things; God arranges it that way. But abiding is the work of the heart, not of the brain. It is the work of the heart clinging to Jesus and resting in Him, a work in which the Holy Spirit joins us to Christ Jesus. Oh, do believe that deeper down than the brain, deep in the inner life, you can abide in Christ, so that every moment you are free, the awareness will come: “Blessed Jesus, I am still in You.” If you will learn to set other work aside for a time and get into this abiding contact with the heavenly Vine, you will find that fruit will come. How does this abiding communion apply to our lives? What does it mean? It means close fellowship with Christ in secret prayer. I am sure there are Christians who really long for the higher life. Sometimes they have received a great blessing, and at times they have known a great inflow of heavenly joy and a great outflow of heavenly gladness — and yet after a while it has passed away. They have not understood that close, personal, real communion with Christ is an absolute necessity for daily life. Take time to be alone with Christ. Nothing in heaven or on earth can free you from the need for that, if you are to be happy and holy Christians. Oh, how many Christians look on being often alone with God as a burden and a tax, a duty and a difficulty! That is the great hindrance to our Christian life everywhere. We need more quiet fellowship with God. And I tell you in the name of the heavenly Vine that you cannot be healthy branches — branches into which the heavenly sap can flow — unless you take plenty of time for communion with God. If you are not willing to sacrifice time to be alone with Him, and to give Him time every day to work in you and to keep up the connection between you and Himself, He cannot give you the blessing of His unbroken fellowship. Jesus Christ asks you to live in close communion with Him. Let every heart say, “O Christ, this is what I long for; this is what I choose.” And He will gladly give it to you. Absolute Surrender And finally, the life of the branch is a life of absolute surrender. This word, absolute surrender, is a great and solemn word, and I believe we do not understand what it means. Yet the little branch preaches it. “Do you have anything to do, little branch, besides bearing grapes?” “No, nothing.” “Are you fit for nothing else?” Fit for nothing! The Bible says that a piece of vine cannot even be used to make a peg; it is fit for nothing but to be burned. “And now, little branch, what do you understand about your relationship to the vine?” “My relationship is simply this: I am utterly given up to the vine, and the vine can give me as much or as little sap as it chooses. Here I am at its disposal, and the vine can do with me whatever it likes.” Oh, friends, we need this absolute surrender to the Lord Jesus Christ. The more I speak, the more I feel that this is one of the hardest points to make clear, and one of the most important and necessary to explain — what this absolute surrender is. It is often easy for a person, or a group of people, to come forward and offer themselves to God for entire consecration and say, “Lord, it is my desire to give myself up entirely to You.” That is very valuable, and it often brings very rich blessing. But the one question I ought to study quietly is: what does absolute surrender mean? It means that, just as literally as Christ was given up entirely to God, I am given up entirely to Christ. Is that too strong? Some think so. Some think it can never be: that just as entirely and absolutely as Christ gave up His life to do nothing but seek the Father’s pleasure and to depend on the Father absolutely and completely, so I am to do nothing but seek the pleasure of Christ. But it really is true. Christ Jesus came to breathe His own Spirit into us, to make us find our very highest happiness in living entirely for God, just as He did. Oh, beloved brothers and sisters, if that is so, then I ought to say: “Yes — as true as it is of that little branch of the vine, so true, by God’s grace, I want it to be of me. I want to live day by day in such a way that Christ can do with me whatever He wills.” Ah, here is the terrible mistake that lies at the root of so much of our religion. A person thinks: “I have my business and my family duties and my responsibilities as a citizen, and I can’t change any of that. And now, alongside all of it, I am to fit in religion and the service of God, as something that will keep me from sin. God help me to do my duties properly!” This is not right. When Christ came, He came and bought the sinner with His blood. If there were a slave market here and I bought a slave, I would take that slave away from his old surroundings to my own house. He would live in my house as my personal property, and I could give him orders all day long. And if he were a faithful slave, he would live as one with no will and no interests of his own; his one concern would be to promote his master’s welfare and honour. In the same way I, who have been bought with the blood of Christ, have been bought to live every day with one thought: how can I please my Master? Oh, we find the Christian life so difficult because we look for God’s blessing while we go on living in our own will. We would be glad to live the Christian life to suit ourselves. We make our own plans and choose our own work, and then we ask the Lord Jesus to come in and make sure that sin does not get too much of a hold on us and that we do not go too far wrong; we ask Him to come in and give us a certain amount of His blessing. But our relationship to Jesus ought to be such that we are entirely at His disposal, and every day we come to Him humbly and plainly and say: “Lord, is there anything in me that is not in line with Your will, that has not been ordered by You, or that is not entirely given up to You?” Oh, if we would wait, and wait patiently, I tell you what the result would be. A relationship between us and Christ would spring up so close and so tender that afterwards we would be amazed at how we could ever have lived with the idea, “I am surrendered to Christ.” We would feel how distant our fellowship with Him had been before, and we would find that He can — and really does — come and take actual possession of us, and give unbroken fellowship all day long. The branch calls us to absolute surrender. I am not speaking now so much about giving up sins. There are people who need that — people with violent tempers, bad habits and actual sins they commit from time to time, which they have never given up into the very bosom of the Lamb of God. I beg you, if you are branches of the living Vine, don’t hold back a single sin. I know there are a great many difficulties about this question of holiness. I know that not everyone thinks exactly the same about it. That would matter relatively little to me if I could see that everyone was honestly longing to be free from every sin. But I am afraid that, without realising it, many hearts make compromises with the idea that we cannot be without sin — that we must sin a little every day, that we cannot help it. Oh, if only people would really cry to God, “Lord, do keep me from sin!” Give yourself utterly to Jesus, and ask Him to do His very utmost for you in keeping you from sin. There is a great deal in our work, in our church and in our surroundings that we found already in the world when we were born into it. It has grown up all around us, and we think it is all right and cannot be changed. We don’t come to the Lord Jesus and ask Him about it. Oh, Christians, I urge you: bring everything into relationship with Jesus and say: “Lord, everything in my life must be in the most complete harmony with my position as a branch of You, the blessed Vine.” Let your surrender to Christ be absolute. I don’t fully understand that word surrender; every so often it takes on new meanings, and from time to time it grows immensely larger. But I urge you to say it out loud: “Absolute surrender to You, O Christ, is what I have chosen.” And Christ will show you what is not according to His mind, and lead you on to deeper and higher blessedness. In conclusion, let me gather it all up in one sentence. Christ Jesus said, “I am the Vine, ye are the branches.” In other words: “I, the living One, who have given myself so completely to you, am the Vine. You cannot trust me too much. I am the almighty Worker, full of divine life and power.” You are the branches of the Lord Jesus Christ. If you are aware in your heart that you are not a strong, healthy, fruit-bearing branch — not closely joined to Jesus, not living in Him as you should — then listen to Him saying: “I am the Vine. I will receive you, I will draw you to myself, I will bless you, I will strengthen you, I will fill you with my Spirit. I, the Vine, have taken you to be my branches; I have given myself utterly to you. Children, give yourselves utterly to me. As God, I have surrendered myself absolutely to you; I became man and died for you so that I might be entirely yours. Come and surrender yourselves entirely to be mine.” What will our answer be? Oh, let it be a prayer from the depths of our hearts that the living Christ may take each one of us and join us closely to Himself. Let our prayer be that He, the living Vine, will so join each of us to Himself that we go away with our hearts singing, “He is my Vine, and I am His branch — I want nothing more — now I have the everlasting Vine.” Then, when you are alone with Him, worship and adore Him, praise Him and trust Him, love Him and wait for His love. “You are my Vine, and I am Your branch. It is enough; my soul is satisfied.” Glory to His blessed name!
